## Question 91 — Same-Origin Policy

**Module:** Module 6 – CORS  
**Difficulty:** ⭐ Easy  
**Experience Level:** 2–5 Years  
**Frequently Asked In:** Google • Meta • Amazon • Microsoft • Netflix • Adobe • Atlassian • Stripe • Uber • Airbnb

### Question
How would you explain **Same-Origin Policy**, model its threats, implement the defense, and review it for production?

### Definition
**Same-Origin Policy** is a frontend security concern that must be evaluated across the browser, application, identity layer, API boundary, dependencies and production operations.

### Overview
Security is a system property. The frontend participates in the attack surface, but sensitive authorization decisions and trust-boundary enforcement must remain server-side.

### Why It Matters
- Prevents account compromise, data exposure and unauthorized actions.
- Reduces exploitable browser and supply-chain attack surface.
- Makes security controls reviewable, testable and observable.

### Browser Behavior
Modern browsers enforce origin boundaries, cookie policies, CSP, permission controls, framing restrictions and secure-context requirements. Security behavior depends on request origin, credentials, headers and browser policy.

### Threat Model
Identify attacker capabilities, protected assets, trust boundaries, entry points, dangerous sinks, authorization decisions and the impact of compromise.

### Attack Flow
```text
Attacker / Untrusted Input
          ↓
      Trust Boundary
          ↓
  Vulnerable Sink / Policy Gap
          ↓
      Security Impact
```

### Internal Security Mechanism
Use browser-enforced controls where possible: Same-Origin Policy, CSP, cookie attributes, CORS, Fetch Metadata, framing protections, Trusted Types and secure transport.

### Architecture
```text
Identity Provider
       ↓
  Secure Session
       ↓
Frontend ─────→ API Gateway
   │                ↓
   └─ Browser       Authorization
      Controls          ↓
                    Backend
```

### Execution Flow
Identify trust boundary → identify attacker-controlled input/state → determine exploit path → apply layered controls → validate with tests and telemetry.

### Real-world Threat
A production application can be exposed when **Same-Origin Policy** is implemented as a convenience feature without explicit trust-boundary analysis, secure defaults and regression tests.

### Real-world Defense
Combine browser controls, server-side validation, least privilege, secure identity/session management, dependency governance and monitoring. Never rely on a single client-side check.

### Production Use Cases
Enterprise SPAs, SaaS applications, banking portals, healthcare systems, e-commerce applications, admin consoles and multi-tenant platforms all require layered security around identity, data and browser execution.

### Enterprise Examples
Security architecture should make authentication, authorization, API boundaries, CSP, dependency controls, logging and incident response explicit rather than scattering security assumptions through components.

### Code Example 1
```ts
// Secure-by-default API wrapper: never interpolate secrets into URLs.
export async function getJson<T>(url: string): Promise<T> {
  const response = await fetch(url, {
    credentials: "same-origin",
    headers: { Accept: "application/json" },
  });

  if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${response.status}`);
  return response.json() as Promise<T>;
}
```

### Code Example 2
```ts
// Validate security-sensitive state at the boundary.
function isAllowedOrigin(origin: string, allowed: readonly string[]) {
  return allowed.includes(origin);
}

console.log(isAllowedOrigin("https://app.example.com", [
  "https://app.example.com",
]));
```

### Secure Production Example
```ts
type SecurityCheck = {
  name: string;
  passed: boolean;
};

const checks: SecurityCheck[] = [
  { name: "HTTPS", passed: true },
  { name: "Authorization server-side", passed: true },
  { name: "Input validation", passed: true },
  { name: "Security logging", passed: true },
];

console.table(checks);
```

### Vulnerable → Secure
❌ Vulnerable: trust browser-controlled roles, concatenate untrusted HTML/URLs, expose long-lived secrets, or disable browser security controls to make integration easier.  
↓  
✅ Secure: enforce authorization server-side, encode/sanitize untrusted content, use hardened session controls, validate origins/redirects and keep security policies explicit.

### Attack Diagram
```text
Attacker
   ↓
Untrusted Data
   ↓
Weak Boundary
   ↓
Browser / API
   ↓
Unauthorized Action or Data Exposure
```

### Defense Diagram
```text
Input Validation
      ↓
Safe Encoding / Sanitization
      ↓
Browser Policy
      ↓
Server Authorization
      ↓
Monitoring
      ↓
Incident Response
```

### Browser Flow Diagram
```text
Request
  ↓
Origin / Credentials
  ↓
Browser Security Policy
  ↓
Network
  ↓
Server Validation
  ↓
Response
  ↓
Safe DOM / State Handling
```

### Advantages
- Reduced attack surface
- Better separation of trust boundaries
- Easier security testing
- Stronger enterprise governance

### Limitations
- Browser controls vary by capability and deployment
- Security policies can add operational complexity
- Legacy integrations may require migration

### Security Trade-offs
| Control | Benefit | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| HttpOnly cookie | Reduces JS cookie access | Requires CSRF/session design |
| CSP | Limits script execution | Requires policy maintenance |
| Strict CORS | Limits cross-origin access | Integration complexity |
| Strong authorization | Limits privilege | More policy management |
| Dependency pinning | Predictability | Update overhead |

### Best Practices
1. Threat-model the feature before implementation.
2. Enforce authorization on the server.
3. Use HTTPS and secure cookie attributes.
4. Avoid dangerous DOM sinks.
5. Apply CSP and Trusted Types where appropriate.
6. Validate redirects, origins and external URLs.
7. Keep dependencies locked and scanned.
8. Log security-relevant events without leaking secrets.
9. Add security gates to CI/CD.

### Anti-patterns
- Client-only authorization
- `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` for untrusted data
- `eval()` or dynamic code execution
- Storing sensitive long-lived credentials in accessible browser storage without a threat-model justification
- Wildcard credentialed CORS
- Disabling CSP because a third-party script is inconvenient

### Common Mistakes
- Confusing CORS with authentication
- Confusing encoding with authorization
- Logging tokens or passwords
- Assuming HTTPS prevents XSS
- Treating JWT signing as permission enforcement

### Debugging Strategy
1. Reproduce the security behavior in an isolated environment.
2. Inspect Network requests and response headers.
3. Inspect cookies, storage and origin information.
4. Check CSP/console violations.
5. Verify server authorization decisions.
6. Review dependency and build output.
7. Add a regression test for the root cause.

### DevTools Demonstration
- **Network:** inspect request credentials, CORS headers, redirects and security headers.
- **Application:** inspect cookies, storage, service workers and permissions.
- **Console:** inspect CSP, mixed-content and browser-policy violations.
- **Sources:** verify dangerous sinks and generated code.

### Security Checklist
- [ ] Threat model completed
- [ ] Trust boundary identified
- [ ] Server-side authorization enforced
- [ ] Sensitive data minimized
- [ ] Browser security policy configured
- [ ] Dependencies scanned
- [ ] Security tests automated
- [ ] Security logging/alerting configured

3. What browser control can reduce the attack surface?
4. What must be enforced server-side?
5. How would you test the defense?
6. What telemetry would detect recurrence?
7. What is the migration strategy for legacy clients?

### Enterprise Architecture Discussion

- [ ] Third-party code is governed

```ts
console.log(isAllowedOrigin("https://app.example.com", [
  "https://app.example.com",
]));
```

### Secure Production Example
```ts
type SecurityCheck = {
  name: string;
  passed: boolean;
};

const checks: SecurityCheck[] = [
  { name: "HTTPS", passed: true },
  { name: "Authorization server-side", passed: true },
  { name: "Input validation", passed: true },
  { name: "Security logging", passed: true },
];

console.table(checks);
```

### Vulnerable → Secure
❌ Vulnerable: trust browser-controlled roles, concatenate untrusted HTML/URLs, expose long-lived secrets, or disable browser security controls to make integration easier.  
↓  
✅ Secure: enforce authorization server-side, encode/sanitize untrusted content, use hardened session controls, validate origins/redirects and keep security policies explicit.

### Attack Diagram
```text
Attacker
   ↓
Untrusted Data
   ↓
Weak Boundary
   ↓
Browser / API
   ↓
Unauthorized Action or Data Exposure
```

### Defense Diagram
```text
Input Validation
      ↓
Safe Encoding / Sanitization
      ↓
Browser Policy
      ↓
Server Authorization
      ↓
Monitoring
      ↓
Incident Response
```

### Browser Flow Diagram
```text
Request
  ↓
Origin / Credentials
  ↓
Browser Security Policy
  ↓
Network
  ↓
Server Validation
  ↓
Response
  ↓
Safe DOM / State Handling
```

### Advantages
- Reduced attack surface
- Better separation of trust boundaries
- Easier security testing
- Stronger enterprise governance

### Limitations
- Browser controls vary by capability and deployment
- Security policies can add operational complexity
- Legacy integrations may require migration

### Security Trade-offs
| Control | Benefit | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| HttpOnly cookie | Reduces JS cookie access | Requires CSRF/session design |
| CSP | Limits script execution | Requires policy maintenance |
| Strict CORS | Limits cross-origin access | Integration complexity |
| Strong authorization | Limits privilege | More policy management |
| Dependency pinning | Predictability | Update overhead |

### Best Practices
1. Threat-model the feature before implementation.
2. Enforce authorization on the server.
3. Use HTTPS and secure cookie attributes.
4. Avoid dangerous DOM sinks.
5. Apply CSP and Trusted Types where appropriate.
6. Validate redirects, origins and external URLs.
7. Keep dependencies locked and scanned.
8. Log security-relevant events without leaking secrets.
9. Add security gates to CI/CD.

### Anti-patterns
- Client-only authorization
- `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` for untrusted data
- `eval()` or dynamic code execution
- Storing sensitive long-lived credentials in accessible browser storage without a threat-model justification
- Wildcard credentialed CORS
- Disabling CSP because a third-party script is inconvenient

### Common Mistakes
- Confusing CORS with authentication
- Confusing encoding with authorization
- Logging tokens or passwords
- Assuming HTTPS prevents XSS
- Treating JWT signing as permission enforcement

### Debugging Strategy
1. Reproduce the security behavior in an isolated environment.
2. Inspect Network requests and response headers.
3. Inspect cookies, storage and origin information.
4. Check CSP/console violations.
5. Verify server authorization decisions.
6. Review dependency and build output.
7. Add a regression test for the root cause.

### DevTools Demonstration
- **Network:** inspect request credentials, CORS headers, redirects and security headers.
- **Application:** inspect cookies, storage, service workers and permissions.
- **Console:** inspect CSP, mixed-content and browser-policy violations.
- **Sources:** verify dangerous sinks and generated code.

### Security Checklist
- [ ] Threat model completed
- [ ] Trust boundary identified
- [ ] Server-side authorization enforced
- [ ] Sensitive data minimized
- [ ] Browser security policy configured
- [ ] Dependencies scanned
- [ ] Security tests automated
- [ ] Security logging/alerting configured

A production application has a security issue involving **Simple requests**. How would you reproduce it safely, identify the root cause, contain the issue and prevent recurrence?

### Senior Follow-up Questions

2. What is the trust boundary?
3. What browser control can reduce the attack surface?
4. What must be enforced server-side?
5. How would you test the defense?
6. What telemetry would detect recurrence?
7. What is the migration strategy for legacy clients?

- [ ] Inputs are untrusted by default
- [ ] Dangerous browser APIs are controlled
- [ ] Third-party code is governed
- [ ] Secrets are not exposed
- [ ] Security policies are versioned

## Question 94 — Preflight

**Module:** Module 6 – CORS  
**Difficulty:** ⭐ Easy  
**Experience Level:** 2–5 Years  
**Frequently Asked In:** Google • Meta • Amazon • Microsoft • Netflix • Adobe • Atlassian • Stripe • Uber • Airbnb

### Question
How would you explain **Preflight**, model its threats, implement the defense, and review it for production?

### Definition
**Preflight** is a frontend security concern that must be evaluated across the browser, application, identity layer, API boundary, dependencies and production operations.

### Overview
Security is a system property. The frontend participates in the attack surface, but sensitive authorization decisions and trust-boundary enforcement must remain server-side.

### Why It Matters
- Prevents account compromise, data exposure and unauthorized actions.
- Reduces exploitable browser and supply-chain attack surface.
- Makes security controls reviewable, testable and observable.

### Browser Behavior
Modern browsers enforce origin boundaries, cookie policies, CSP, permission controls, framing restrictions and secure-context requirements. Security behavior depends on request origin, credentials, headers and browser policy.

### Threat Model
Identify attacker capabilities, protected assets, trust boundaries, entry points, dangerous sinks, authorization decisions and the impact of compromise.

### Attack Flow
```text
Attacker / Untrusted Input
          ↓
      Trust Boundary
          ↓
  Vulnerable Sink / Policy Gap
          ↓
      Security Impact
```

### Internal Security Mechanism
Use browser-enforced controls where possible: Same-Origin Policy, CSP, cookie attributes, CORS, Fetch Metadata, framing protections, Trusted Types and secure transport.

### Architecture
```text
Identity Provider
       ↓
  Secure Session
       ↓
Frontend ─────→ API Gateway
   │                ↓
   └─ Browser       Authorization
      Controls          ↓
                    Backend
```

### Execution Flow
Identify trust boundary → identify attacker-controlled input/state → determine exploit path → apply layered controls → validate with tests and telemetry.

### Real-world Threat
A production application can be exposed when **Preflight** is implemented as a convenience feature without explicit trust-boundary analysis, secure defaults and regression tests.

### Real-world Defense
Combine browser controls, server-side validation, least privilege, secure identity/session management, dependency governance and monitoring. Never rely on a single client-side check.

### Production Use Cases
Enterprise SPAs, SaaS applications, banking portals, healthcare systems, e-commerce applications, admin consoles and multi-tenant platforms all require layered security around identity, data and browser execution.

### Enterprise Examples
Security architecture should make authentication, authorization, API boundaries, CSP, dependency controls, logging and incident response explicit rather than scattering security assumptions through components.

### Code Example 1
```ts
// Secure-by-default API wrapper: never interpolate secrets into URLs.
export async function getJson<T>(url: string): Promise<T> {
  const response = await fetch(url, {
    credentials: "same-origin",
    headers: { Accept: "application/json" },
  });

  if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${response.status}`);
  return response.json() as Promise<T>;
}
```

```ts
  { name: "Security logging", passed: true },
];

console.table(checks);
```

      ↓

## Question 96 — Access-Control-Allow-Credentials

**Module:** Module 6 – CORS  
**Difficulty:** ⭐ Easy  
**Experience Level:** 2–5 Years  
**Frequently Asked In:** Google • Meta • Amazon • Microsoft • Netflix • Adobe • Atlassian • Stripe • Uber • Airbnb

### Question
How would you explain **Access-Control-Allow-Credentials**, model its threats, implement the defense, and review it for production?

### Definition
**Access-Control-Allow-Credentials** is a frontend security concern that must be evaluated across the browser, application, identity layer, API boundary, dependencies and production operations.

### Overview
Security is a system property. The frontend participates in the attack surface, but sensitive authorization decisions and trust-boundary enforcement must remain server-side.

### Why It Matters
- Prevents account compromise, data exposure and unauthorized actions.
- Reduces exploitable browser and supply-chain attack surface.
- Makes security controls reviewable, testable and observable.

### Browser Behavior
Modern browsers enforce origin boundaries, cookie policies, CSP, permission controls, framing restrictions and secure-context requirements. Security behavior depends on request origin, credentials, headers and browser policy.

### Threat Model
Identify attacker capabilities, protected assets, trust boundaries, entry points, dangerous sinks, authorization decisions and the impact of compromise.

### Attack Flow
```text
Attacker / Untrusted Input
          ↓
      Trust Boundary
          ↓
  Vulnerable Sink / Policy Gap
          ↓
      Security Impact
```

### Internal Security Mechanism
Use browser-enforced controls where possible: Same-Origin Policy, CSP, cookie attributes, CORS, Fetch Metadata, framing protections, Trusted Types and secure transport.

### Architecture
```text
Identity Provider
       ↓
  Secure Session
       ↓
Frontend ─────→ API Gateway
   │                ↓
   └─ Browser       Authorization
      Controls          ↓
                    Backend
```

### Execution Flow
Identify trust boundary → identify attacker-controlled input/state → determine exploit path → apply layered controls → validate with tests and telemetry.

### Real-world Threat
A production application can be exposed when **Access-Control-Allow-Credentials** is implemented as a convenience feature without explicit trust-boundary analysis, secure defaults and regression tests.

### Real-world Defense
Combine browser controls, server-side validation, least privilege, secure identity/session management, dependency governance and monitoring. Never rely on a single client-side check.

### Production Use Cases
Enterprise SPAs, SaaS applications, banking portals, healthcare systems, e-commerce applications, admin consoles and multi-tenant platforms all require layered security around identity, data and browser execution.

### Enterprise Examples
Security architecture should make authentication, authorization, API boundaries, CSP, dependency controls, logging and incident response explicit rather than scattering security assumptions through components.

### Code Example 1
```ts
// Secure-by-default API wrapper: never interpolate secrets into URLs.
export async function getJson<T>(url: string): Promise<T> {
  const response = await fetch(url, {
    credentials: "same-origin",
    headers: { Accept: "application/json" },
  });

  if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${response.status}`);
  return response.json() as Promise<T>;
}
```

### Code Example 2
```ts
// Validate security-sensitive state at the boundary.
function isAllowedOrigin(origin: string, allowed: readonly string[]) {
  return allowed.includes(origin);
}

console.log(isAllowedOrigin("https://app.example.com", [
  "https://app.example.com",
]));
```

### Secure Production Example
```ts
type SecurityCheck = {
  name: string;
  passed: boolean;
};

const checks: SecurityCheck[] = [
  { name: "HTTPS", passed: true },
  { name: "Authorization server-side", passed: true },
  { name: "Input validation", passed: true },
  { name: "Security logging", passed: true },
];

console.table(checks);
```

### Vulnerable → Secure
❌ Vulnerable: trust browser-controlled roles, concatenate untrusted HTML/URLs, expose long-lived secrets, or disable browser security controls to make integration easier.  
↓  
✅ Secure: enforce authorization server-side, encode/sanitize untrusted content, use hardened session controls, validate origins/redirects and keep security policies explicit.

### Attack Diagram
```text
Attacker
   ↓
Untrusted Data
   ↓
Weak Boundary
   ↓
Browser / API
   ↓
Unauthorized Action or Data Exposure
```

### Defense Diagram
```text
Input Validation
      ↓
Safe Encoding / Sanitization
      ↓
Browser Policy
      ↓
Server Authorization
      ↓
Monitoring
      ↓
Incident Response
```

### Browser Flow Diagram
```text
Request
  ↓
Origin / Credentials
  ↓
Browser Security Policy
  ↓
Network
  ↓
Server Validation
  ↓
Response
  ↓
Safe DOM / State Handling
```

### Advantages
- Reduced attack surface
- Better separation of trust boundaries
- Easier security testing
- Stronger enterprise governance

### Limitations
- Browser controls vary by capability and deployment
- Security policies can add operational complexity
- Legacy integrations may require migration

### Security Trade-offs
| Control | Benefit | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| HttpOnly cookie | Reduces JS cookie access | Requires CSRF/session design |
| CSP | Limits script execution | Requires policy maintenance |
| Strict CORS | Limits cross-origin access | Integration complexity |
| Strong authorization | Limits privilege | More policy management |
| Dependency pinning | Predictability | Update overhead |

### Best Practices
1. Threat-model the feature before implementation.
2. Enforce authorization on the server.
3. Use HTTPS and secure cookie attributes.
4. Avoid dangerous DOM sinks.
5. Apply CSP and Trusted Types where appropriate.
6. Validate redirects, origins and external URLs.
7. Keep dependencies locked and scanned.
8. Log security-relevant events without leaking secrets.
9. Add security gates to CI/CD.

### Anti-patterns
- Client-only authorization
- `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` for untrusted data
- `eval()` or dynamic code execution
- Storing sensitive long-lived credentials in accessible browser storage without a threat-model justification
- Wildcard credentialed CORS
- Disabling CSP because a third-party script is inconvenient

### Common Mistakes
- Confusing CORS with authentication
- Confusing encoding with authorization
- Logging tokens or passwords
- Assuming HTTPS prevents XSS
- Treating JWT signing as permission enforcement

### Debugging Strategy
1. Reproduce the security behavior in an isolated environment.
2. Inspect Network requests and response headers.
3. Inspect cookies, storage and origin information.
4. Check CSP/console violations.
5. Verify server authorization decisions.
6. Review dependency and build output.
7. Add a regression test for the root cause.

### DevTools Demonstration
- **Network:** inspect request credentials, CORS headers, redirects and security headers.
- **Application:** inspect cookies, storage, service workers and permissions.
- **Console:** inspect CSP, mixed-content and browser-policy violations.
- **Sources:** verify dangerous sinks and generated code.

### Security Checklist
- [ ] Threat model completed
- [ ] Trust boundary identified
- [ ] Server-side authorization enforced
- [ ] Sensitive data minimized
- [ ] Browser security policy configured
- [ ] Dependencies scanned
- [ ] Security tests automated
- [ ] Security logging/alerting configured

### Scenario-Based Interview Question
A production application has a security issue involving **Access-Control-Allow-Credentials**. How would you reproduce it safely, identify the root cause, contain the issue and prevent recurrence?

### Senior Follow-up Questions
1. What is the attacker capability?
2. What is the trust boundary?
3. What browser control can reduce the attack surface?
4. What must be enforced server-side?
5. How would you test the defense?
6. What telemetry would detect recurrence?
7. What is the migration strategy for legacy clients?

### Enterprise Architecture Discussion
At Staff/Principal level, design security as a platform capability: centralized identity, policy enforcement, secure API clients, security headers, dependency governance, audit logging, threat modeling, CI/CD gates and incident response.

### Security Review Checklist
- [ ] Authentication is explicit
- [ ] Authorization is server-side
- [ ] Inputs are untrusted by default
- [ ] Dangerous browser APIs are controlled
- [ ] Third-party code is governed
- [ ] Secrets are not exposed
- [ ] Security policies are versioned

### 30-second Interview Answer
For **Access-Control-Allow-Credentials**, I would first identify the attacker and trust boundary, then apply browser and server-side controls in layers. I would validate the defense with automated security tests and monitor production for regression.

### 2-minute Interview Answer
I treat **Access-Control-Allow-Credentials** as a threat-modeling problem rather than a code-only problem. I identify attacker capabilities, data flows and trust boundaries, choose secure browser/platform controls, enforce sensitive decisions server-side, test abuse cases, and add CI/CD and production monitoring.

### 5-minute Deep Explanation
At Staff/Principal level, discuss **Access-Control-Allow-Credentials** through identity, browser isolation, API boundaries, secure coding, supply-chain risk, observability, incident response, compliance and organizational governance. The strongest answer explains not just the mitigation but its limitations, operational trade-offs and how the organization prevents recurrence.

### Assignments
Create a threat model for a feature involving **Access-Control-Allow-Credentials**, list attacker capabilities, trust boundaries, attack paths, mitigations and residual risk.

### Mini Project
Build a secure React 19 + TypeScript application with authenticated routes, server-enforced authorization, hardened session handling, CSP, safe rendering, secure API calls, dependency scanning and security event logging.

### MCQs
1. Where should authorization ultimately be enforced?  
A. CSS  B. Client router only  C. Server/API  D. Browser local state  
**Answer: C**
2. Which cookie attribute prevents JavaScript access?  
A. Secure  B. HttpOnly  C. Path  D. Domain  
**Answer: B**
3. Which control reduces script injection impact?  
A. CSP  B. DNS  C. JSON.parse only  D. CORS alone  
**Answer: A**
4. What is a major supply-chain defense?  
A. Ignore lock files  B. Dependency scanning and provenance  C. Disable HTTPS  D. Remove tests  
**Answer: B**
5. What is the safest assumption for external input?  
A. Trusted  B. Encoded already  C. Untrusted  D. Internal  
**Answer: C**

### Hands-on Exercise
Audit a demo application for **Access-Control-Allow-Credentials**. Document the vulnerable trust boundary, reproduce the issue safely, apply a defense and add a regression test.

### Secure Coding Exercise
Implement one secure boundary: validate an origin/redirect, render untrusted text safely, enforce a permission check server-side, or configure a hardened session policy.

### Revision Notes
- Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: attacker → trust boundary → exploit → impact → layered defense → test → monitor.
- Browser security controls complement—not replace—server-side authorization.
- Security must survive deployment, dependency updates and production incidents.

### Cheat Sheet
**Identity → Authorization → Transport → Browser Policy → Safe Input/Output → API Validation → Dependencies → Monitoring.**

## Question 99 — Expose headers

**Module:** Module 6 – CORS  
**Difficulty:** ⭐ Easy  
**Experience Level:** 2–5 Years  
**Frequently Asked In:** Google • Meta • Amazon • Microsoft • Netflix • Adobe • Atlassian • Stripe • Uber • Airbnb

### Question
How would you explain **Expose headers**, model its threats, implement the defense, and review it for production?

### Definition
**Expose headers** is a frontend security concern that must be evaluated across the browser, application, identity layer, API boundary, dependencies and production operations.

### Overview
Security is a system property. The frontend participates in the attack surface, but sensitive authorization decisions and trust-boundary enforcement must remain server-side.

### Why It Matters
- Prevents account compromise, data exposure and unauthorized actions.
- Reduces exploitable browser and supply-chain attack surface.
- Makes security controls reviewable, testable and observable.

### Browser Behavior
Modern browsers enforce origin boundaries, cookie policies, CSP, permission controls, framing restrictions and secure-context requirements. Security behavior depends on request origin, credentials, headers and browser policy.

### Threat Model
Identify attacker capabilities, protected assets, trust boundaries, entry points, dangerous sinks, authorization decisions and the impact of compromise.

### Attack Flow
```text
Attacker / Untrusted Input
          ↓
      Trust Boundary
          ↓
  Vulnerable Sink / Policy Gap
          ↓
      Security Impact
```

### Internal Security Mechanism
Use browser-enforced controls where possible: Same-Origin Policy, CSP, cookie attributes, CORS, Fetch Metadata, framing protections, Trusted Types and secure transport.

### Architecture
```text
Identity Provider
       ↓
  Secure Session
       ↓
Frontend ─────→ API Gateway
   │                ↓
   └─ Browser       Authorization
      Controls          ↓
                    Backend
```

### Execution Flow
Identify trust boundary → identify attacker-controlled input/state → determine exploit path → apply layered controls → validate with tests and telemetry.

### Real-world Threat
A production application can be exposed when **Expose headers** is implemented as a convenience feature without explicit trust-boundary analysis, secure defaults and regression tests.

### Real-world Defense
Combine browser controls, server-side validation, least privilege, secure identity/session management, dependency governance and monitoring. Never rely on a single client-side check.

### Production Use Cases
Enterprise SPAs, SaaS applications, banking portals, healthcare systems, e-commerce applications, admin consoles and multi-tenant platforms all require layered security around identity, data and browser execution.

### Enterprise Examples
Security architecture should make authentication, authorization, API boundaries, CSP, dependency controls, logging and incident response explicit rather than scattering security assumptions through components.

### Code Example 1
```ts
// Secure-by-default API wrapper: never interpolate secrets into URLs.
export async function getJson<T>(url: string): Promise<T> {
  const response = await fetch(url, {
    credentials: "same-origin",
    headers: { Accept: "application/json" },
  });

  if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${response.status}`);
  return response.json() as Promise<T>;
}
```

### Code Example 2
```ts
// Validate security-sensitive state at the boundary.
function isAllowedOrigin(origin: string, allowed: readonly string[]) {
  return allowed.includes(origin);
}

console.log(isAllowedOrigin("https://app.example.com", [
  "https://app.example.com",
]));
```

### Secure Production Example
```ts
type SecurityCheck = {
  name: string;
  passed: boolean;
};

const checks: SecurityCheck[] = [
  { name: "HTTPS", passed: true },
  { name: "Authorization server-side", passed: true },
  { name: "Input validation", passed: true },
  { name: "Security logging", passed: true },
];

console.table(checks);
```

### Vulnerable → Secure
❌ Vulnerable: trust browser-controlled roles, concatenate untrusted HTML/URLs, expose long-lived secrets, or disable browser security controls to make integration easier.  
↓  
✅ Secure: enforce authorization server-side, encode/sanitize untrusted content, use hardened session controls, validate origins/redirects and keep security policies explicit.

### Attack Diagram
```text
Attacker
   ↓
Untrusted Data
   ↓
Weak Boundary
   ↓
Browser / API
   ↓
Unauthorized Action or Data Exposure
```

### Defense Diagram
```text
Input Validation
      ↓
Safe Encoding / Sanitization
      ↓
Browser Policy
      ↓
Server Authorization
      ↓
Monitoring
      ↓
Incident Response
```

### Browser Flow Diagram
```text
Request
  ↓
Origin / Credentials
  ↓
Browser Security Policy
  ↓
Network
  ↓
Server Validation
  ↓
Response
  ↓
Safe DOM / State Handling
```

### Advantages
- Reduced attack surface
- Better separation of trust boundaries
- Easier security testing
- Stronger enterprise governance

### Limitations
- Browser controls vary by capability and deployment
- Security policies can add operational complexity
- Legacy integrations may require migration

### Security Trade-offs
| Control | Benefit | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| HttpOnly cookie | Reduces JS cookie access | Requires CSRF/session design |
| CSP | Limits script execution | Requires policy maintenance |
| Strict CORS | Limits cross-origin access | Integration complexity |
| Strong authorization | Limits privilege | More policy management |
| Dependency pinning | Predictability | Update overhead |

### Best Practices
1. Threat-model the feature before implementation.
2. Enforce authorization on the server.
3. Use HTTPS and secure cookie attributes.
4. Avoid dangerous DOM sinks.
5. Apply CSP and Trusted Types where appropriate.
6. Validate redirects, origins and external URLs.
7. Keep dependencies locked and scanned.
8. Log security-relevant events without leaking secrets.
9. Add security gates to CI/CD.

### Anti-patterns
- Client-only authorization
- `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` for untrusted data
- `eval()` or dynamic code execution
- Storing sensitive long-lived credentials in accessible browser storage without a threat-model justification
- Wildcard credentialed CORS
- Disabling CSP because a third-party script is inconvenient

### Common Mistakes
- Confusing CORS with authentication
- Confusing encoding with authorization
- Logging tokens or passwords
- Assuming HTTPS prevents XSS
- Treating JWT signing as permission enforcement

### Debugging Strategy
1. Reproduce the security behavior in an isolated environment.
2. Inspect Network requests and response headers.
3. Inspect cookies, storage and origin information.
4. Check CSP/console violations.
5. Verify server authorization decisions.
6. Review dependency and build output.
7. Add a regression test for the root cause.

### DevTools Demonstration
- **Network:** inspect request credentials, CORS headers, redirects and security headers.
- **Application:** inspect cookies, storage, service workers and permissions.
- **Console:** inspect CSP, mixed-content and browser-policy violations.
- **Sources:** verify dangerous sinks and generated code.

### Security Checklist
- [ ] Threat model completed
- [ ] Trust boundary identified
- [ ] Server-side authorization enforced
- [ ] Sensitive data minimized
- [ ] Browser security policy configured
- [ ] Dependencies scanned
- [ ] Security tests automated
- [ ] Security logging/alerting configured

```text
Browser Policy
      ↓
Server Authorization
      ↓
Monitoring
      ↓
Incident Response
```

### Browser Flow Diagram
```text
Request
  ↓
Origin / Credentials
  ↓
Browser Security Policy
  ↓
Network
  ↓
Server Validation
  ↓
Response
  ↓
Safe DOM / State Handling
```

### Advantages
- Reduced attack surface
- Better separation of trust boundaries
- Easier security testing
- Stronger enterprise governance

### Limitations
- Browser controls vary by capability and deployment
- Security policies can add operational complexity
- Legacy integrations may require migration

### Security Trade-offs
| Control | Benefit | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| HttpOnly cookie | Reduces JS cookie access | Requires CSRF/session design |
| CSP | Limits script execution | Requires policy maintenance |
| Strict CORS | Limits cross-origin access | Integration complexity |
| Strong authorization | Limits privilege | More policy management |
| Dependency pinning | Predictability | Update overhead |

### Best Practices
1. Threat-model the feature before implementation.
2. Enforce authorization on the server.
3. Use HTTPS and secure cookie attributes.
4. Avoid dangerous DOM sinks.
5. Apply CSP and Trusted Types where appropriate.
6. Validate redirects, origins and external URLs.
7. Keep dependencies locked and scanned.
8. Log security-relevant events without leaking secrets.
9. Add security gates to CI/CD.

### Anti-patterns
- Client-only authorization
- `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` for untrusted data
- `eval()` or dynamic code execution
- Storing sensitive long-lived credentials in accessible browser storage without a threat-model justification
- Wildcard credentialed CORS
- Disabling CSP because a third-party script is inconvenient

### Common Mistakes
- Confusing CORS with authentication
- Confusing encoding with authorization
- Logging tokens or passwords
- Assuming HTTPS prevents XSS
- Treating JWT signing as permission enforcement

### Debugging Strategy
1. Reproduce the security behavior in an isolated environment.
2. Inspect Network requests and response headers.
3. Inspect cookies, storage and origin information.
4. Check CSP/console violations.
5. Verify server authorization decisions.
6. Review dependency and build output.
7. Add a regression test for the root cause.

### DevTools Demonstration
- **Network:** inspect request credentials, CORS headers, redirects and security headers.
- **Application:** inspect cookies, storage, service workers and permissions.
- **Console:** inspect CSP, mixed-content and browser-policy violations.
- **Sources:** verify dangerous sinks and generated code.

### Security Checklist
- [ ] Threat model completed
- [ ] Trust boundary identified
- [ ] Server-side authorization enforced
- [ ] Sensitive data minimized
- [ ] Browser security policy configured
- [ ] Dependencies scanned
- [ ] Security tests automated
- [ ] Security logging/alerting configured

## Question 102 — Dynamic origin validation

**Module:** Module 6 – CORS  
**Difficulty:** ⭐⭐ Medium  
**Experience Level:** 5–8 Years  
**Frequently Asked In:** Google • Meta • Amazon • Microsoft • Netflix • Adobe • Atlassian • Stripe • Uber • Airbnb

### Question
How would you explain **Dynamic origin validation**, model its threats, implement the defense, and review it for production?

### Definition
**Dynamic origin validation** is a frontend security concern that must be evaluated across the browser, application, identity layer, API boundary, dependencies and production operations.

### Overview
Security is a system property. The frontend participates in the attack surface, but sensitive authorization decisions and trust-boundary enforcement must remain server-side.

### Why It Matters
- Prevents account compromise, data exposure and unauthorized actions.
- Reduces exploitable browser and supply-chain attack surface.
- Makes security controls reviewable, testable and observable.

### Browser Behavior
Modern browsers enforce origin boundaries, cookie policies, CSP, permission controls, framing restrictions and secure-context requirements. Security behavior depends on request origin, credentials, headers and browser policy.

### Threat Model
Identify attacker capabilities, protected assets, trust boundaries, entry points, dangerous sinks, authorization decisions and the impact of compromise.

### Attack Flow
```text
Attacker / Untrusted Input
          ↓
      Trust Boundary
          ↓
  Vulnerable Sink / Policy Gap
          ↓
      Security Impact
```

### Internal Security Mechanism
Use browser-enforced controls where possible: Same-Origin Policy, CSP, cookie attributes, CORS, Fetch Metadata, framing protections, Trusted Types and secure transport.

### Architecture
```text
Identity Provider
       ↓
  Secure Session
       ↓
Frontend ─────→ API Gateway
   │                ↓
   └─ Browser       Authorization
      Controls          ↓
                    Backend
```

### Execution Flow
Identify trust boundary → identify attacker-controlled input/state → determine exploit path → apply layered controls → validate with tests and telemetry.

### Real-world Threat
A production application can be exposed when **Dynamic origin validation** is implemented as a convenience feature without explicit trust-boundary analysis, secure defaults and regression tests.

### Real-world Defense
Combine browser controls, server-side validation, least privilege, secure identity/session management, dependency governance and monitoring. Never rely on a single client-side check.

### Production Use Cases
Enterprise SPAs, SaaS applications, banking portals, healthcare systems, e-commerce applications, admin consoles and multi-tenant platforms all require layered security around identity, data and browser execution.

### Enterprise Examples
Security architecture should make authentication, authorization, API boundaries, CSP, dependency controls, logging and incident response explicit rather than scattering security assumptions through components.

### Code Example 1
```ts
// Secure-by-default API wrapper: never interpolate secrets into URLs.
export async function getJson<T>(url: string): Promise<T> {
  const response = await fetch(url, {
    credentials: "same-origin",
    headers: { Accept: "application/json" },
  });

  if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${response.status}`);
  return response.json() as Promise<T>;
}
```

### Code Example 2
```ts
// Validate security-sensitive state at the boundary.
function isAllowedOrigin(origin: string, allowed: readonly string[]) {
  return allowed.includes(origin);
}

console.log(isAllowedOrigin("https://app.example.com", [
  "https://app.example.com",
]));
```

### Secure Production Example
```ts
type SecurityCheck = {
  name: string;
  passed: boolean;
};

const checks: SecurityCheck[] = [
  { name: "HTTPS", passed: true },
  { name: "Authorization server-side", passed: true },
  { name: "Input validation", passed: true },
  { name: "Security logging", passed: true },
];

console.table(checks);
```

### Vulnerable → Secure
❌ Vulnerable: trust browser-controlled roles, concatenate untrusted HTML/URLs, expose long-lived secrets, or disable browser security controls to make integration easier.  
↓  
✅ Secure: enforce authorization server-side, encode/sanitize untrusted content, use hardened session controls, validate origins/redirects and keep security policies explicit.

### Attack Diagram
```text
Attacker
   ↓
Untrusted Data
   ↓
Weak Boundary
   ↓
Browser / API
   ↓
Unauthorized Action or Data Exposure
```

### Defense Diagram
```text
Input Validation
      ↓
Safe Encoding / Sanitization
      ↓
Browser Policy
      ↓
Server Authorization
      ↓
Monitoring
      ↓
Incident Response
```

### Browser Flow Diagram
```text
Request
  ↓
Origin / Credentials
  ↓
Browser Security Policy
  ↓
Network
  ↓
Server Validation
  ↓
Response
  ↓
Safe DOM / State Handling
```

- Stronger enterprise governance

```text
  Vulnerable Sink / Policy Gap
          ↓
      Security Impact
```

### Internal Security Mechanism
Use browser-enforced controls where possible: Same-Origin Policy, CSP, cookie attributes, CORS, Fetch Metadata, framing protections, Trusted Types and secure transport.

### Architecture
```text
Identity Provider
       ↓
  Secure Session
       ↓
Frontend ─────→ API Gateway
   │                ↓
   └─ Browser       Authorization
      Controls          ↓
                    Backend
```

### Execution Flow
Identify trust boundary → identify attacker-controlled input/state → determine exploit path → apply layered controls → validate with tests and telemetry.

### Real-world Threat
A production application can be exposed when **Wildcard origins** is implemented as a convenience feature without explicit trust-boundary analysis, secure defaults and regression tests.

### Real-world Defense
Combine browser controls, server-side validation, least privilege, secure identity/session management, dependency governance and monitoring. Never rely on a single client-side check.

### Production Use Cases
Enterprise SPAs, SaaS applications, banking portals, healthcare systems, e-commerce applications, admin consoles and multi-tenant platforms all require layered security around identity, data and browser execution.

### Enterprise Examples
Security architecture should make authentication, authorization, API boundaries, CSP, dependency controls, logging and incident response explicit rather than scattering security assumptions through components.

### Code Example 1
```ts
// Secure-by-default API wrapper: never interpolate secrets into URLs.
export async function getJson<T>(url: string): Promise<T> {
  const response = await fetch(url, {
    credentials: "same-origin",
    headers: { Accept: "application/json" },
  });

  if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${response.status}`);
  return response.json() as Promise<T>;
}
```

### Code Example 2
```ts
// Validate security-sensitive state at the boundary.
function isAllowedOrigin(origin: string, allowed: readonly string[]) {
  return allowed.includes(origin);
}

console.log(isAllowedOrigin("https://app.example.com", [
  "https://app.example.com",
]));
```

### Secure Production Example
```ts
type SecurityCheck = {
  name: string;
  passed: boolean;
};

const checks: SecurityCheck[] = [
  { name: "HTTPS", passed: true },
  { name: "Authorization server-side", passed: true },
  { name: "Input validation", passed: true },
  { name: "Security logging", passed: true },
];

console.table(checks);
```

### Vulnerable → Secure
❌ Vulnerable: trust browser-controlled roles, concatenate untrusted HTML/URLs, expose long-lived secrets, or disable browser security controls to make integration easier.  
↓  
✅ Secure: enforce authorization server-side, encode/sanitize untrusted content, use hardened session controls, validate origins/redirects and keep security policies explicit.

### Attack Diagram
```text
Attacker
   ↓
Untrusted Data
   ↓
Weak Boundary
   ↓
Browser / API
   ↓
Unauthorized Action or Data Exposure
```

### Defense Diagram
```text
Input Validation
      ↓
Safe Encoding / Sanitization
      ↓
Browser Policy
      ↓
Server Authorization
      ↓
Monitoring
      ↓
Incident Response
```

### Browser Flow Diagram
```text
Request
  ↓
Origin / Credentials
  ↓
Browser Security Policy
  ↓
Network
  ↓
Server Validation
  ↓
Response
  ↓
Safe DOM / State Handling
```

### Advantages
- Reduced attack surface
- Better separation of trust boundaries
- Easier security testing
- Stronger enterprise governance

### Limitations
- Browser controls vary by capability and deployment
- Security policies can add operational complexity
- Legacy integrations may require migration

### Security Trade-offs
| Control | Benefit | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| HttpOnly cookie | Reduces JS cookie access | Requires CSRF/session design |
| CSP | Limits script execution | Requires policy maintenance |
| Strict CORS | Limits cross-origin access | Integration complexity |
| Strong authorization | Limits privilege | More policy management |
| Dependency pinning | Predictability | Update overhead |

### Best Practices
1. Threat-model the feature before implementation.
2. Enforce authorization on the server.
3. Use HTTPS and secure cookie attributes.
4. Avoid dangerous DOM sinks.
5. Apply CSP and Trusted Types where appropriate.
6. Validate redirects, origins and external URLs.
7. Keep dependencies locked and scanned.
8. Log security-relevant events without leaking secrets.
9. Add security gates to CI/CD.

### Anti-patterns
- Client-only authorization
- `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` for untrusted data
- `eval()` or dynamic code execution
- Storing sensitive long-lived credentials in accessible browser storage without a threat-model justification
- Wildcard credentialed CORS
- Disabling CSP because a third-party script is inconvenient

### Common Mistakes
- Confusing CORS with authentication
- Confusing encoding with authorization
- Logging tokens or passwords
- Assuming HTTPS prevents XSS
- Treating JWT signing as permission enforcement

### Debugging Strategy
1. Reproduce the security behavior in an isolated environment.
2. Inspect Network requests and response headers.
3. Inspect cookies, storage and origin information.
4. Check CSP/console violations.
5. Verify server authorization decisions.
6. Review dependency and build output.
7. Add a regression test for the root cause.

### DevTools Demonstration
- **Network:** inspect request credentials, CORS headers, redirects and security headers.
- **Application:** inspect cookies, storage, service workers and permissions.
- **Console:** inspect CSP, mixed-content and browser-policy violations.
- **Sources:** verify dangerous sinks and generated code.

### Security Checklist
- [ ] Threat model completed
- [ ] Trust boundary identified
- [ ] Server-side authorization enforced
- [ ] Sensitive data minimized
- [ ] Browser security policy configured
- [ ] Dependencies scanned
- [ ] Security tests automated
- [ ] Security logging/alerting configured

- [ ] Inputs are untrusted by default

## Question 107 — default-src

**Module:** Module 7 – Content Security Policy  
**Difficulty:** ⭐⭐ Medium  
**Experience Level:** 5–8 Years  
**Frequently Asked In:** Google • Meta • Amazon • Microsoft • Netflix • Adobe • Atlassian • Stripe • Uber • Airbnb

### Question
How would you explain **default-src**, model its threats, implement the defense, and review it for production?

### Definition
**default-src** is a frontend security concern that must be evaluated across the browser, application, identity layer, API boundary, dependencies and production operations.

### Overview
Security is a system property. The frontend participates in the attack surface, but sensitive authorization decisions and trust-boundary enforcement must remain server-side.

### Why It Matters
- Prevents account compromise, data exposure and unauthorized actions.
- Reduces exploitable browser and supply-chain attack surface.
- Makes security controls reviewable, testable and observable.

### Browser Behavior
Modern browsers enforce origin boundaries, cookie policies, CSP, permission controls, framing restrictions and secure-context requirements. Security behavior depends on request origin, credentials, headers and browser policy.

### Threat Model
Identify attacker capabilities, protected assets, trust boundaries, entry points, dangerous sinks, authorization decisions and the impact of compromise.

### Attack Flow
```text
Attacker / Untrusted Input
          ↓
      Trust Boundary
          ↓
  Vulnerable Sink / Policy Gap
          ↓
      Security Impact
```

### Internal Security Mechanism
Use browser-enforced controls where possible: Same-Origin Policy, CSP, cookie attributes, CORS, Fetch Metadata, framing protections, Trusted Types and secure transport.

### Architecture
```text
Identity Provider
       ↓
  Secure Session
       ↓
Frontend ─────→ API Gateway
   │                ↓
   └─ Browser       Authorization
      Controls          ↓
                    Backend
```

### Execution Flow
Identify trust boundary → identify attacker-controlled input/state → determine exploit path → apply layered controls → validate with tests and telemetry.

### Real-world Threat
A production application can be exposed when **default-src** is implemented as a convenience feature without explicit trust-boundary analysis, secure defaults and regression tests.

### Real-world Defense
Combine browser controls, server-side validation, least privilege, secure identity/session management, dependency governance and monitoring. Never rely on a single client-side check.

### Production Use Cases
Enterprise SPAs, SaaS applications, banking portals, healthcare systems, e-commerce applications, admin consoles and multi-tenant platforms all require layered security around identity, data and browser execution.

### Enterprise Examples
Security architecture should make authentication, authorization, API boundaries, CSP, dependency controls, logging and incident response explicit rather than scattering security assumptions through components.

### Code Example 1
```ts
// Secure-by-default API wrapper: never interpolate secrets into URLs.
export async function getJson<T>(url: string): Promise<T> {
  const response = await fetch(url, {
    credentials: "same-origin",
    headers: { Accept: "application/json" },
  });

  if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${response.status}`);
  return response.json() as Promise<T>;
}
```

### Code Example 2
```ts
// Validate security-sensitive state at the boundary.
function isAllowedOrigin(origin: string, allowed: readonly string[]) {
  return allowed.includes(origin);
}

console.log(isAllowedOrigin("https://app.example.com", [
  "https://app.example.com",
]));
```

### Secure Production Example
```ts
type SecurityCheck = {
  name: string;
  passed: boolean;
};

const checks: SecurityCheck[] = [
  { name: "HTTPS", passed: true },
  { name: "Authorization server-side", passed: true },
  { name: "Input validation", passed: true },
  { name: "Security logging", passed: true },
];

console.table(checks);
```

### Vulnerable → Secure
❌ Vulnerable: trust browser-controlled roles, concatenate untrusted HTML/URLs, expose long-lived secrets, or disable browser security controls to make integration easier.  
↓  
✅ Secure: enforce authorization server-side, encode/sanitize untrusted content, use hardened session controls, validate origins/redirects and keep security policies explicit.

### Attack Diagram
```text
Attacker
   ↓
Untrusted Data
   ↓
Weak Boundary
   ↓
Browser / API
   ↓
Unauthorized Action or Data Exposure
```

### Defense Diagram
```text
Input Validation
      ↓
Safe Encoding / Sanitization
      ↓
Browser Policy
      ↓
Server Authorization
      ↓
Monitoring
      ↓
Incident Response
```

### Browser Flow Diagram
```text
Request
  ↓
Origin / Credentials
  ↓
Browser Security Policy
  ↓
Network
  ↓
Server Validation
  ↓
Response
  ↓
Safe DOM / State Handling
```

### Advantages
- Reduced attack surface
- Better separation of trust boundaries
- Easier security testing
- Stronger enterprise governance

### Limitations
- Browser controls vary by capability and deployment
- Security policies can add operational complexity
- Legacy integrations may require migration

### Security Trade-offs
| Control | Benefit | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| HttpOnly cookie | Reduces JS cookie access | Requires CSRF/session design |
| CSP | Limits script execution | Requires policy maintenance |
| Strict CORS | Limits cross-origin access | Integration complexity |
| Strong authorization | Limits privilege | More policy management |
| Dependency pinning | Predictability | Update overhead |

### Best Practices
1. Threat-model the feature before implementation.
2. Enforce authorization on the server.
3. Use HTTPS and secure cookie attributes.
4. Avoid dangerous DOM sinks.
5. Apply CSP and Trusted Types where appropriate.
6. Validate redirects, origins and external URLs.
7. Keep dependencies locked and scanned.
8. Log security-relevant events without leaking secrets.
9. Add security gates to CI/CD.

### Anti-patterns
- Client-only authorization
- `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` for untrusted data
- `eval()` or dynamic code execution
- Storing sensitive long-lived credentials in accessible browser storage without a threat-model justification
- Wildcard credentialed CORS
- Disabling CSP because a third-party script is inconvenient

### Common Mistakes
- Confusing CORS with authentication
- Confusing encoding with authorization
- Logging tokens or passwords
- Assuming HTTPS prevents XSS
- Treating JWT signing as permission enforcement

### Debugging Strategy
1. Reproduce the security behavior in an isolated environment.
2. Inspect Network requests and response headers.
3. Inspect cookies, storage and origin information.
4. Check CSP/console violations.
5. Verify server authorization decisions.
6. Review dependency and build output.
7. Add a regression test for the root cause.

### DevTools Demonstration
- **Network:** inspect request credentials, CORS headers, redirects and security headers.
- **Application:** inspect cookies, storage, service workers and permissions.
- **Console:** inspect CSP, mixed-content and browser-policy violations.
- **Sources:** verify dangerous sinks and generated code.

### Security Checklist
- [ ] Threat model completed
- [ ] Trust boundary identified
- [ ] Server-side authorization enforced
- [ ] Sensitive data minimized
- [ ] Browser security policy configured
- [ ] Dependencies scanned
- [ ] Security tests automated
- [ ] Security logging/alerting configured

### Scenario-Based Interview Question
A production application has a security issue involving **default-src**. How would you reproduce it safely, identify the root cause, contain the issue and prevent recurrence?

### Senior Follow-up Questions
1. What is the attacker capability?
2. What is the trust boundary?
3. What browser control can reduce the attack surface?
4. What must be enforced server-side?
5. How would you test the defense?
6. What telemetry would detect recurrence?
7. What is the migration strategy for legacy clients?

### Enterprise Architecture Discussion
At Staff/Principal level, design security as a platform capability: centralized identity, policy enforcement, secure API clients, security headers, dependency governance, audit logging, threat modeling, CI/CD gates and incident response.

### Security Review Checklist
- [ ] Authentication is explicit
- [ ] Authorization is server-side
- [ ] Inputs are untrusted by default
- [ ] Dangerous browser APIs are controlled
- [ ] Third-party code is governed
- [ ] Secrets are not exposed
- [ ] Security policies are versioned

### 30-second Interview Answer
For **default-src**, I would first identify the attacker and trust boundary, then apply browser and server-side controls in layers. I would validate the defense with automated security tests and monitor production for regression.

### 2-minute Interview Answer
I treat **default-src** as a threat-modeling problem rather than a code-only problem. I identify attacker capabilities, data flows and trust boundaries, choose secure browser/platform controls, enforce sensitive decisions server-side, test abuse cases, and add CI/CD and production monitoring.

### 5-minute Deep Explanation
At Staff/Principal level, discuss **default-src** through identity, browser isolation, API boundaries, secure coding, supply-chain risk, observability, incident response, compliance and organizational governance. The strongest answer explains not just the mitigation but its limitations, operational trade-offs and how the organization prevents recurrence.

**Answer: B**
3. Which control reduces script injection impact?  
A. CSP  B. DNS  C. JSON.parse only  D. CORS alone  
**Answer: A**
4. What is a major supply-chain defense?

**Answer: B**
5. What is the safest assumption for external input?  
A. Trusted  B. Encoded already  C. Untrusted  D. Internal  
**Answer: C**

Audit a demo application for **default-src**. Document the vulnerable trust boundary, reproduce the issue safely, apply a defense and add a regression test.

- Client-only authorization
- `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` for untrusted data
- `eval()` or dynamic code execution
- Storing sensitive long-lived credentials in accessible browser storage without a threat-model justification
- Wildcard credentialed CORS
- Disabling CSP because a third-party script is inconvenient

### Common Mistakes
- Confusing CORS with authentication
- Confusing encoding with authorization
- Logging tokens or passwords
- Assuming HTTPS prevents XSS
- Treating JWT signing as permission enforcement

### Debugging Strategy
1. Reproduce the security behavior in an isolated environment.
2. Inspect Network requests and response headers.
3. Inspect cookies, storage and origin information.
4. Check CSP/console violations.
5. Verify server authorization decisions.
6. Review dependency and build output.
7. Add a regression test for the root cause.

### DevTools Demonstration
- **Network:** inspect request credentials, CORS headers, redirects and security headers.
- **Application:** inspect cookies, storage, service workers and permissions.
- **Console:** inspect CSP, mixed-content and browser-policy violations.
- **Sources:** verify dangerous sinks and generated code.

### Security Checklist
- [ ] Threat model completed
- [ ] Trust boundary identified
- [ ] Server-side authorization enforced
- [ ] Sensitive data minimized
- [ ] Browser security policy configured
- [ ] Dependencies scanned
- [ ] Security tests automated
- [ ] Security logging/alerting configured

### Scenario-Based Interview Question
A production application has a security issue involving **style-src**. How would you reproduce it safely, identify the root cause, contain the issue and prevent recurrence?

### Senior Follow-up Questions

2. What is the trust boundary?
3. What browser control can reduce the attack surface?
4. What must be enforced server-side?
5. How would you test the defense?
6. What telemetry would detect recurrence?
7. What is the migration strategy for legacy clients?

### Enterprise Architecture Discussion
At Staff/Principal level, design security as a platform capability: centralized identity, policy enforcement, secure API clients, security headers, dependency governance, audit logging, threat modeling, CI/CD gates and incident response.

### Security Review Checklist
- [ ] Authentication is explicit
- [ ] Authorization is server-side
- [ ] Inputs are untrusted by default
- [ ] Dangerous browser APIs are controlled
- [ ] Third-party code is governed
- [ ] Secrets are not exposed
- [ ] Security policies are versioned

## Question 110 — img-src

**Module:** Module 7 – Content Security Policy  
**Difficulty:** ⭐⭐ Medium  
**Experience Level:** 5–8 Years  
**Frequently Asked In:** Google • Meta • Amazon • Microsoft • Netflix • Adobe • Atlassian • Stripe • Uber • Airbnb

### Question
How would you explain **img-src**, model its threats, implement the defense, and review it for production?

### Definition
**img-src** is a frontend security concern that must be evaluated across the browser, application, identity layer, API boundary, dependencies and production operations.

### Overview
Security is a system property. The frontend participates in the attack surface, but sensitive authorization decisions and trust-boundary enforcement must remain server-side.

### Why It Matters
- Prevents account compromise, data exposure and unauthorized actions.
- Reduces exploitable browser and supply-chain attack surface.
- Makes security controls reviewable, testable and observable.

### Browser Behavior
Modern browsers enforce origin boundaries, cookie policies, CSP, permission controls, framing restrictions and secure-context requirements. Security behavior depends on request origin, credentials, headers and browser policy.

### Threat Model
Identify attacker capabilities, protected assets, trust boundaries, entry points, dangerous sinks, authorization decisions and the impact of compromise.

### Attack Flow
```text
Attacker / Untrusted Input
          ↓
      Trust Boundary
          ↓
  Vulnerable Sink / Policy Gap
          ↓
      Security Impact
```

### Internal Security Mechanism
Use browser-enforced controls where possible: Same-Origin Policy, CSP, cookie attributes, CORS, Fetch Metadata, framing protections, Trusted Types and secure transport.

### Architecture
```text
Identity Provider
       ↓
  Secure Session
       ↓
Frontend ─────→ API Gateway
   │                ↓
   └─ Browser       Authorization
      Controls          ↓
                    Backend
```

### Execution Flow
Identify trust boundary → identify attacker-controlled input/state → determine exploit path → apply layered controls → validate with tests and telemetry.

### Real-world Threat
A production application can be exposed when **img-src** is implemented as a convenience feature without explicit trust-boundary analysis, secure defaults and regression tests.

### Real-world Defense
Combine browser controls, server-side validation, least privilege, secure identity/session management, dependency governance and monitoring. Never rely on a single client-side check.

### Production Use Cases
Enterprise SPAs, SaaS applications, banking portals, healthcare systems, e-commerce applications, admin consoles and multi-tenant platforms all require layered security around identity, data and browser execution.

### Enterprise Examples
Security architecture should make authentication, authorization, API boundaries, CSP, dependency controls, logging and incident response explicit rather than scattering security assumptions through components.

### Code Example 1
```ts
// Secure-by-default API wrapper: never interpolate secrets into URLs.
export async function getJson<T>(url: string): Promise<T> {
  const response = await fetch(url, {
    credentials: "same-origin",
    headers: { Accept: "application/json" },
  });

  if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${response.status}`);
  return response.json() as Promise<T>;
}
```

### Code Example 2
```ts
// Validate security-sensitive state at the boundary.
function isAllowedOrigin(origin: string, allowed: readonly string[]) {
  return allowed.includes(origin);
}

console.log(isAllowedOrigin("https://app.example.com", [
  "https://app.example.com",
]));
```

### Secure Production Example
```ts
type SecurityCheck = {
  name: string;
  passed: boolean;
};

const checks: SecurityCheck[] = [
  { name: "HTTPS", passed: true },
  { name: "Authorization server-side", passed: true },
  { name: "Input validation", passed: true },
  { name: "Security logging", passed: true },
];

console.table(checks);
```

### Vulnerable → Secure
❌ Vulnerable: trust browser-controlled roles, concatenate untrusted HTML/URLs, expose long-lived secrets, or disable browser security controls to make integration easier.  
↓  
✅ Secure: enforce authorization server-side, encode/sanitize untrusted content, use hardened session controls, validate origins/redirects and keep security policies explicit.

### Attack Diagram
```text
Attacker
   ↓
Untrusted Data
   ↓
Weak Boundary
   ↓
Browser / API
   ↓
Unauthorized Action or Data Exposure
```

### Defense Diagram
```text
Input Validation
      ↓
Safe Encoding / Sanitization
      ↓
Browser Policy
      ↓
Server Authorization
      ↓
Monitoring
      ↓
Incident Response
```

### Browser Flow Diagram
```text
Request
  ↓
Origin / Credentials
  ↓
Browser Security Policy
  ↓
Network
  ↓
Server Validation
  ↓
Response
  ↓
Safe DOM / State Handling
```

### Advantages
- Reduced attack surface
- Better separation of trust boundaries
- Easier security testing
- Stronger enterprise governance

### Limitations
- Browser controls vary by capability and deployment
- Security policies can add operational complexity
- Legacy integrations may require migration

### Security Trade-offs
| Control | Benefit | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| HttpOnly cookie | Reduces JS cookie access | Requires CSRF/session design |
| CSP | Limits script execution | Requires policy maintenance |
| Strict CORS | Limits cross-origin access | Integration complexity |
| Strong authorization | Limits privilege | More policy management |
| Dependency pinning | Predictability | Update overhead |

### Best Practices
1. Threat-model the feature before implementation.
2. Enforce authorization on the server.
3. Use HTTPS and secure cookie attributes.
4. Avoid dangerous DOM sinks.
5. Apply CSP and Trusted Types where appropriate.
6. Validate redirects, origins and external URLs.
7. Keep dependencies locked and scanned.
8. Log security-relevant events without leaking secrets.
9. Add security gates to CI/CD.

### Anti-patterns
- Client-only authorization
- `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` for untrusted data
- `eval()` or dynamic code execution
- Storing sensitive long-lived credentials in accessible browser storage without a threat-model justification
- Wildcard credentialed CORS
- Disabling CSP because a third-party script is inconvenient

### Common Mistakes
- Confusing CORS with authentication
- Confusing encoding with authorization
- Logging tokens or passwords
- Assuming HTTPS prevents XSS
- Treating JWT signing as permission enforcement

### Debugging Strategy
1. Reproduce the security behavior in an isolated environment.
2. Inspect Network requests and response headers.
3. Inspect cookies, storage and origin information.
4. Check CSP/console violations.
5. Verify server authorization decisions.
6. Review dependency and build output.
7. Add a regression test for the root cause.

### DevTools Demonstration
- **Network:** inspect request credentials, CORS headers, redirects and security headers.
- **Application:** inspect cookies, storage, service workers and permissions.
- **Console:** inspect CSP, mixed-content and browser-policy violations.
- **Sources:** verify dangerous sinks and generated code.

### Security Checklist
- [ ] Threat model completed
- [ ] Trust boundary identified
- [ ] Server-side authorization enforced
- [ ] Sensitive data minimized
- [ ] Browser security policy configured
- [ ] Dependencies scanned
- [ ] Security tests automated
- [ ] Security logging/alerting configured

4. What must be enforced server-side?
5. How would you test the defense?
6. What telemetry would detect recurrence?
7. What is the migration strategy for legacy clients?

### Enterprise Architecture Discussion

```ts
    headers: { Accept: "application/json" },
  });

  if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${response.status}`);
  return response.json() as Promise<T>;
}
```

### Code Example 2
```ts
// Validate security-sensitive state at the boundary.
function isAllowedOrigin(origin: string, allowed: readonly string[]) {
  return allowed.includes(origin);
}

console.log(isAllowedOrigin("https://app.example.com", [
  "https://app.example.com",
]));
```

### Secure Production Example
```ts
type SecurityCheck = {
  name: string;
  passed: boolean;
};

const checks: SecurityCheck[] = [
  { name: "HTTPS", passed: true },
  { name: "Authorization server-side", passed: true },
  { name: "Input validation", passed: true },
  { name: "Security logging", passed: true },
];

console.table(checks);
```

### Vulnerable → Secure
❌ Vulnerable: trust browser-controlled roles, concatenate untrusted HTML/URLs, expose long-lived secrets, or disable browser security controls to make integration easier.  
↓  
✅ Secure: enforce authorization server-side, encode/sanitize untrusted content, use hardened session controls, validate origins/redirects and keep security policies explicit.

### Attack Diagram
```text
Attacker
   ↓
Untrusted Data
   ↓
Weak Boundary
   ↓
Browser / API
   ↓
Unauthorized Action or Data Exposure
```

### Defense Diagram
```text
Input Validation
      ↓
Safe Encoding / Sanitization
      ↓
Browser Policy
      ↓
Server Authorization
      ↓
Monitoring
      ↓
Incident Response
```

### Browser Flow Diagram
```text
Request
  ↓
Origin / Credentials
  ↓
Browser Security Policy
  ↓
Network
  ↓
Server Validation
  ↓
Response
  ↓
Safe DOM / State Handling
```

### Advantages
- Reduced attack surface
- Better separation of trust boundaries
- Easier security testing
- Stronger enterprise governance

### Limitations
- Browser controls vary by capability and deployment
- Security policies can add operational complexity
- Legacy integrations may require migration

### Security Trade-offs
| Control | Benefit | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| HttpOnly cookie | Reduces JS cookie access | Requires CSRF/session design |
| CSP | Limits script execution | Requires policy maintenance |
| Strict CORS | Limits cross-origin access | Integration complexity |
| Strong authorization | Limits privilege | More policy management |
| Dependency pinning | Predictability | Update overhead |

### Best Practices
1. Threat-model the feature before implementation.
2. Enforce authorization on the server.
3. Use HTTPS and secure cookie attributes.
4. Avoid dangerous DOM sinks.
5. Apply CSP and Trusted Types where appropriate.
6. Validate redirects, origins and external URLs.
7. Keep dependencies locked and scanned.
8. Log security-relevant events without leaking secrets.
9. Add security gates to CI/CD.

### Anti-patterns
- Client-only authorization
- `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` for untrusted data
- `eval()` or dynamic code execution
- Storing sensitive long-lived credentials in accessible browser storage without a threat-model justification
- Wildcard credentialed CORS
- Disabling CSP because a third-party script is inconvenient

### Common Mistakes
- Confusing CORS with authentication
- Confusing encoding with authorization
- Logging tokens or passwords
- Assuming HTTPS prevents XSS
- Treating JWT signing as permission enforcement

### Debugging Strategy
1. Reproduce the security behavior in an isolated environment.
2. Inspect Network requests and response headers.
3. Inspect cookies, storage and origin information.
4. Check CSP/console violations.
5. Verify server authorization decisions.
6. Review dependency and build output.
7. Add a regression test for the root cause.

### DevTools Demonstration
- **Network:** inspect request credentials, CORS headers, redirects and security headers.
- **Application:** inspect cookies, storage, service workers and permissions.
- **Console:** inspect CSP, mixed-content and browser-policy violations.
- **Sources:** verify dangerous sinks and generated code.

### Security Checklist
- [ ] Threat model completed
- [ ] Trust boundary identified
- [ ] Server-side authorization enforced
- [ ] Sensitive data minimized
- [ ] Browser security policy configured
- [ ] Dependencies scanned
- [ ] Security tests automated
- [ ] Security logging/alerting configured

### Scenario-Based Interview Question
A production application has a security issue involving **frame-ancestors**. How would you reproduce it safely, identify the root cause, contain the issue and prevent recurrence?

### Senior Follow-up Questions
1. What is the attacker capability?
2. What is the trust boundary?
3. What browser control can reduce the attack surface?
4. What must be enforced server-side?
5. How would you test the defense?
6. What telemetry would detect recurrence?
7. What is the migration strategy for legacy clients?

- [ ] Authorization is server-side
- [ ] Inputs are untrusted by default
- [ ] Dangerous browser APIs are controlled
- [ ] Third-party code is governed
- [ ] Secrets are not exposed
- [ ] Security policies are versioned

### 2-minute Interview Answer

At Staff/Principal level, discuss **frame-ancestors** through identity, browser isolation, API boundaries, secure coding, supply-chain risk, observability, incident response, compliance and organizational governance. ## Question 113 — object-src

**Module:** Module 7 – Content Security Policy  
**Difficulty:** ⭐⭐ Medium  
**Experience Level:** 5–8 Years  
**Frequently Asked In:** Google • Meta • Amazon • Microsoft • Netflix • Adobe • Atlassian • Stripe • Uber • Airbnb

### Question
How would you explain **object-src**, model its threats, implement the defense, and review it for production?

### Definition
**object-src** is a frontend security concern that must be evaluated across the browser, application, identity layer, API boundary, dependencies and production operations.

### Overview
Security is a system property. The frontend participates in the attack surface, but sensitive authorization decisions and trust-boundary enforcement must remain server-side.

### Why It Matters
- Prevents account compromise, data exposure and unauthorized actions.
- Reduces exploitable browser and supply-chain attack surface.
- Makes security controls reviewable, testable and observable.

### Browser Behavior
Modern browsers enforce origin boundaries, cookie policies, CSP, permission controls, framing restrictions and secure-context requirements. Security behavior depends on request origin, credentials, headers and browser policy.

### Threat Model
Identify attacker capabilities, protected assets, trust boundaries, entry points, dangerous sinks, authorization decisions and the impact of compromise.

### Attack Flow
```text
Attacker / Untrusted Input
          ↓
      Trust Boundary
          ↓
  Vulnerable Sink / Policy Gap
          ↓
      Security Impact
```

### Internal Security Mechanism
Use browser-enforced controls where possible: Same-Origin Policy, CSP, cookie attributes, CORS, Fetch Metadata, framing protections, Trusted Types and secure transport.

### Architecture
```text
Identity Provider
       ↓
  Secure Session
       ↓
Frontend ─────→ API Gateway
   │                ↓
   └─ Browser       Authorization
      Controls          ↓
                    Backend
```

### Execution Flow
Identify trust boundary → identify attacker-controlled input/state → determine exploit path → apply layered controls → validate with tests and telemetry.

### Real-world Threat
A production application can be exposed when **object-src** is implemented as a convenience feature without explicit trust-boundary analysis, secure defaults and regression tests.

### Real-world Defense
Combine browser controls, server-side validation, least privilege, secure identity/session management, dependency governance and monitoring. Never rely on a single client-side check.

### Production Use Cases
Enterprise SPAs, SaaS applications, banking portals, healthcare systems, e-commerce applications, admin consoles and multi-tenant platforms all require layered security around identity, data and browser execution.

### Enterprise Examples
Security architecture should make authentication, authorization, API boundaries, CSP, dependency controls, logging and incident response explicit rather than scattering security assumptions through components.
