## Question 324 — Production incident response

**Module:** Module 19 – Real-world Security Scenarios  
**Difficulty:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐ Senior  
**Experience Level:** 12+ Years  
**Frequently Asked In:** Google • Meta • Amazon • Microsoft • Netflix • Adobe • Atlassian • Stripe • Uber • Airbnb

### Question
How would you explain **Production incident response**, model its threats, implement the defense, and review it for production?

### Definition
**Production incident response** is a frontend security concern that must be evaluated across the browser, application, identity layer, API boundary, dependencies and production operations.

### Overview
Security is a system property. The frontend participates in the attack surface, but sensitive authorization decisions and trust-boundary enforcement must remain server-side.

### Why It Matters
- Prevents account compromise, data exposure and unauthorized actions.
- Reduces exploitable browser and supply-chain attack surface.
- Makes security controls reviewable, testable and observable.

### Browser Behavior
Modern browsers enforce origin boundaries, cookie policies, CSP, permission controls, framing restrictions and secure-context requirements. Security behavior depends on request origin, credentials, headers and browser policy.

### Threat Model
Identify attacker capabilities, protected assets, trust boundaries, entry points, dangerous sinks, authorization decisions and the impact of compromise.

### Attack Flow
```text
Attacker / Untrusted Input
          ↓
      Trust Boundary
          ↓
  Vulnerable Sink / Policy Gap
          ↓
      Security Impact
```

### Internal Security Mechanism
Use browser-enforced controls where possible: Same-Origin Policy, CSP, cookie attributes, CORS, Fetch Metadata, framing protections, Trusted Types and secure transport.

### Architecture
```text
Identity Provider
       ↓
  Secure Session
       ↓
Frontend ─────→ API Gateway
   │                ↓
   └─ Browser       Authorization
      Controls          ↓
                    Backend
```

### Execution Flow
Identify trust boundary → identify attacker-controlled input/state → determine exploit path → apply layered controls → validate with tests and telemetry.

### Real-world Threat
A production application can be exposed when **Production incident response** is implemented as a convenience feature without explicit trust-boundary analysis, secure defaults and regression tests.

### Real-world Defense
Combine browser controls, server-side validation, least privilege, secure identity/session management, dependency governance and monitoring. Never rely on a single client-side check.

### Production Use Cases
Enterprise SPAs, SaaS applications, banking portals, healthcare systems, e-commerce applications, admin consoles and multi-tenant platforms all require layered security around identity, data and browser execution.

### Enterprise Examples
Security architecture should make authentication, authorization, API boundaries, CSP, dependency controls, logging and incident response explicit rather than scattering security assumptions through components.

### Code Example 1
```ts
// Secure-by-default API wrapper: never interpolate secrets into URLs.
export async function getJson<T>(url: string): Promise<T> {
  const response = await fetch(url, {
    credentials: "same-origin",
    headers: { Accept: "application/json" },
  });

  if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${response.status}`);
  return response.json() as Promise<T>;
}
```

### Code Example 2
```ts
// Validate security-sensitive state at the boundary.
function isAllowedOrigin(origin: string, allowed: readonly string[]) {
  return allowed.includes(origin);
}

console.log(isAllowedOrigin("https://app.example.com", [
  "https://app.example.com",
]));
```

### Secure Production Example
```ts
type SecurityCheck = {
  name: string;
  passed: boolean;
};

const checks: SecurityCheck[] = [
  { name: "HTTPS", passed: true },
  { name: "Authorization server-side", passed: true },
  { name: "Input validation", passed: true },
  { name: "Security logging", passed: true },
];

console.table(checks);
```

### Vulnerable → Secure
❌ Vulnerable: trust browser-controlled roles, concatenate untrusted HTML/URLs, expose long-lived secrets, or disable browser security controls to make integration easier.  
↓  
✅ Secure: enforce authorization server-side, encode/sanitize untrusted content, use hardened session controls, validate origins/redirects and keep security policies explicit.

### Attack Diagram
```text
Attacker
   ↓
Untrusted Data
   ↓
Weak Boundary
   ↓
Browser / API
   ↓
Unauthorized Action or Data Exposure
```

### Defense Diagram
```text
Input Validation
      ↓
Safe Encoding / Sanitization
      ↓
Browser Policy
      ↓
Server Authorization
      ↓
Monitoring
      ↓
Incident Response
```

### Browser Flow Diagram
```text
Request
  ↓
Origin / Credentials
  ↓
Browser Security Policy
  ↓
Network
  ↓
Server Validation
  ↓
Response
  ↓
Safe DOM / State Handling
```

### Advantages
- Reduced attack surface
- Better separation of trust boundaries
- Easier security testing
- Stronger enterprise governance

### Limitations
- Browser controls vary by capability and deployment
- Security policies can add operational complexity
- Legacy integrations may require migration

### Security Trade-offs
| Control | Benefit | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| HttpOnly cookie | Reduces JS cookie access | Requires CSRF/session design |
| CSP | Limits script execution | Requires policy maintenance |
| Strict CORS | Limits cross-origin access | Integration complexity |
| Strong authorization | Limits privilege | More policy management |
| Dependency pinning | Predictability | Update overhead |

### Best Practices
1. Threat-model the feature before implementation.
2. Enforce authorization on the server.
3. Use HTTPS and secure cookie attributes.
4. Avoid dangerous DOM sinks.
5. Apply CSP and Trusted Types where appropriate.
6. Validate redirects, origins and external URLs.
7. Keep dependencies locked and scanned.
8. Log security-relevant events without leaking secrets.
9. Add security gates to CI/CD.

### Anti-patterns
- Client-only authorization
- `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` for untrusted data
- `eval()` or dynamic code execution
- Storing sensitive long-lived credentials in accessible browser storage without a threat-model justification
- Wildcard credentialed CORS
- Disabling CSP because a third-party script is inconvenient

### Common Mistakes
- Confusing CORS with authentication
- Confusing encoding with authorization
- Logging tokens or passwords
- Assuming HTTPS prevents XSS
- Treating JWT signing as permission enforcement

### Debugging Strategy
1. Reproduce the security behavior in an isolated environment.
2. Inspect Network requests and response headers.
3. Inspect cookies, storage and origin information.
4. Check CSP/console violations.
5. Verify server authorization decisions.
6. Review dependency and build output.
7. Add a regression test for the root cause.

### DevTools Demonstration
- **Network:** inspect request credentials, CORS headers, redirects and security headers.
- **Application:** inspect cookies, storage, service workers and permissions.
- **Console:** inspect CSP, mixed-content and browser-policy violations.
- **Sources:** verify dangerous sinks and generated code.

### Security Checklist
- [ ] Threat model completed
- [ ] Trust boundary identified
- [ ] Server-side authorization enforced
- [ ] Sensitive data minimized
- [ ] Browser security policy configured
- [ ] Dependencies scanned
- [ ] Security tests automated
- [ ] Security logging/alerting configured

### Scenario-Based Interview Question
A production application has a security issue involving **Production incident response**. How would you reproduce it safely, identify the root cause, contain the issue and prevent recurrence?

### Senior Follow-up Questions
1. What is the attacker capability?
2. What is the trust boundary?
3. What browser control can reduce the attack surface?
4. What must be enforced server-side?
5. How would you test the defense?
6. What telemetry would detect recurrence?
7. What is the migration strategy for legacy clients?

### Enterprise Architecture Discussion
At Staff/Principal level, design security as a platform capability: centralized identity, policy enforcement, secure API clients, security headers, dependency governance, audit logging, threat modeling, CI/CD gates and incident response.

### Security Review Checklist

- [ ] Authorization is server-side
- [ ] Inputs are untrusted by default
- [ ] Dangerous browser APIs are controlled
- [ ] Third-party code is governed
- [ ] Secrets are not exposed
- [ ] Security policies are versioned


### Browser Flow Diagram
```text
Request
  ↓
Origin / Credentials
  ↓
Browser Security Policy
  ↓
Network
  ↓
Server Validation
  ↓
Response
  ↓
Safe DOM / State Handling
```

### Advantages
- Reduced attack surface
- Better separation of trust boundaries
- Easier security testing
- Stronger enterprise governance

### Limitations
- Browser controls vary by capability and deployment
- Security policies can add operational complexity
- Legacy integrations may require migration

### Security Trade-offs
| Control | Benefit | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| HttpOnly cookie | Reduces JS cookie access | Requires CSRF/session design |
| CSP | Limits script execution | Requires policy maintenance |
| Strict CORS | Limits cross-origin access | Integration complexity |
| Strong authorization | Limits privilege | More policy management |
| Dependency pinning | Predictability | Update overhead |

### Best Practices
1. Threat-model the feature before implementation.
2. Enforce authorization on the server.
3. Use HTTPS and secure cookie attributes.
4. Avoid dangerous DOM sinks.
5. Apply CSP and Trusted Types where appropriate.
6. Validate redirects, origins and external URLs.
7. Keep dependencies locked and scanned.
8. Log security-relevant events without leaking secrets.
9. Add security gates to CI/CD.

### Anti-patterns
- Client-only authorization
- `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` for untrusted data
- `eval()` or dynamic code execution
- Storing sensitive long-lived credentials in accessible browser storage without a threat-model justification
- Wildcard credentialed CORS
- Disabling CSP because a third-party script is inconvenient

### Common Mistakes
- Confusing CORS with authentication
- Confusing encoding with authorization
- Logging tokens or passwords
- Assuming HTTPS prevents XSS
- Treating JWT signing as permission enforcement

### Debugging Strategy
1. Reproduce the security behavior in an isolated environment.
2. Inspect Network requests and response headers.
3. Inspect cookies, storage and origin information.
4. Check CSP/console violations.
5. Verify server authorization decisions.
6. Review dependency and build output.
7. Add a regression test for the root cause.

### DevTools Demonstration
- **Network:** inspect request credentials, CORS headers, redirects and security headers.
- **Application:** inspect cookies, storage, service workers and permissions.
- **Console:** inspect CSP, mixed-content and browser-policy violations.
- **Sources:** verify dangerous sinks and generated code.

### Security Checklist
- [ ] Threat model completed
- [ ] Trust boundary identified
- [ ] Server-side authorization enforced
- [ ] Sensitive data minimized
- [ ] Browser security policy configured
- [ ] Dependencies scanned
- [ ] Security tests automated
- [ ] Security logging/alerting configured

## Question 327 — Authentication revision

**Module:** Module 20 – Final Revision  
**Difficulty:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ Principal  
**Experience Level:** 12+ Years  
**Frequently Asked In:** Google • Meta • Amazon • Microsoft • Netflix • Adobe • Atlassian • Stripe • Uber • Airbnb

### Question
How would you explain **Authentication revision**, model its threats, implement the defense, and review it for production?

### Definition
**Authentication revision** is a frontend security concern that must be evaluated across the browser, application, identity layer, API boundary, dependencies and production operations.

### Overview
Security is a system property. The frontend participates in the attack surface, but sensitive authorization decisions and trust-boundary enforcement must remain server-side.

### Why It Matters
- Prevents account compromise, data exposure and unauthorized actions.
- Reduces exploitable browser and supply-chain attack surface.
- Makes security controls reviewable, testable and observable.

### Browser Behavior
Modern browsers enforce origin boundaries, cookie policies, CSP, permission controls, framing restrictions and secure-context requirements. Security behavior depends on request origin, credentials, headers and browser policy.

### Threat Model
Identify attacker capabilities, protected assets, trust boundaries, entry points, dangerous sinks, authorization decisions and the impact of compromise.

### Attack Flow
```text
Attacker / Untrusted Input
          ↓
      Trust Boundary
          ↓
  Vulnerable Sink / Policy Gap
          ↓
      Security Impact
```

### Internal Security Mechanism
Use browser-enforced controls where possible: Same-Origin Policy, CSP, cookie attributes, CORS, Fetch Metadata, framing protections, Trusted Types and secure transport.

### Architecture
```text
Identity Provider
       ↓
  Secure Session
       ↓
Frontend ─────→ API Gateway
   │                ↓
   └─ Browser       Authorization
      Controls          ↓
                    Backend
```

### Execution Flow
Identify trust boundary → identify attacker-controlled input/state → determine exploit path → apply layered controls → validate with tests and telemetry.

### Real-world Threat
A production application can be exposed when **Authentication revision** is implemented as a convenience feature without explicit trust-boundary analysis, secure defaults and regression tests.

### Real-world Defense
Combine browser controls, server-side validation, least privilege, secure identity/session management, dependency governance and monitoring. Never rely on a single client-side check.

### Production Use Cases
Enterprise SPAs, SaaS applications, banking portals, healthcare systems, e-commerce applications, admin consoles and multi-tenant platforms all require layered security around identity, data and browser execution.

### Enterprise Examples
Security architecture should make authentication, authorization, API boundaries, CSP, dependency controls, logging and incident response explicit rather than scattering security assumptions through components.

### Code Example 1
```ts
// Secure-by-default API wrapper: never interpolate secrets into URLs.
export async function getJson<T>(url: string): Promise<T> {
  const response = await fetch(url, {
    credentials: "same-origin",
    headers: { Accept: "application/json" },
  });

  if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${response.status}`);
  return response.json() as Promise<T>;
}
```

### Code Example 2
```ts
// Validate security-sensitive state at the boundary.
function isAllowedOrigin(origin: string, allowed: readonly string[]) {
  return allowed.includes(origin);
}

console.log(isAllowedOrigin("https://app.example.com", [
  "https://app.example.com",
]));
```

### Secure Production Example
```ts
type SecurityCheck = {
  name: string;
  passed: boolean;
};

const checks: SecurityCheck[] = [
  { name: "HTTPS", passed: true },
  { name: "Authorization server-side", passed: true },
  { name: "Input validation", passed: true },
  { name: "Security logging", passed: true },
];

console.table(checks);
```

### Vulnerable → Secure
❌ Vulnerable: trust browser-controlled roles, concatenate untrusted HTML/URLs, expose long-lived secrets, or disable browser security controls to make integration easier.  
↓  
✅ Secure: enforce authorization server-side, encode/sanitize untrusted content, use hardened session controls, validate origins/redirects and keep security policies explicit.

### Attack Diagram
```text
Attacker
   ↓
Untrusted Data
   ↓
Weak Boundary
   ↓
Browser / API
   ↓
Unauthorized Action or Data Exposure
```

### Defense Diagram
```text
Input Validation
      ↓
Safe Encoding / Sanitization
      ↓
Browser Policy
      ↓
Server Authorization
      ↓
Monitoring
      ↓
Incident Response
```

### Browser Flow Diagram
```text
Request
  ↓
Origin / Credentials
  ↓
Browser Security Policy
  ↓
Network
  ↓
Server Validation
  ↓
Response
  ↓
Safe DOM / State Handling
```

- Stronger enterprise governance

Use browser-enforced controls where possible: Same-Origin Policy, CSP, cookie attributes, CORS, Fetch Metadata, framing protections, Trusted Types and secure transport.

### Architecture
```text
Identity Provider
       ↓
  Secure Session
       ↓
Frontend ─────→ API Gateway
   │                ↓
   └─ Browser       Authorization
      Controls          ↓
                    Backend
```

### Execution Flow
Identify trust boundary → identify attacker-controlled input/state → determine exploit path → apply layered controls → validate with tests and telemetry.

### Real-world Threat
A production application can be exposed when **XSS revision** is implemented as a convenience feature without explicit trust-boundary analysis, secure defaults and regression tests.

### Real-world Defense
Combine browser controls, server-side validation, least privilege, secure identity/session management, dependency governance and monitoring. Never rely on a single client-side check.

### Production Use Cases
Enterprise SPAs, SaaS applications, banking portals, healthcare systems, e-commerce applications, admin consoles and multi-tenant platforms all require layered security around identity, data and browser execution.

### Enterprise Examples
Security architecture should make authentication, authorization, API boundaries, CSP, dependency controls, logging and incident response explicit rather than scattering security assumptions through components.

### Code Example 1
```tsx
// ❌ Vulnerable: untrusted HTML is interpreted by the browser.
// element.innerHTML = userInput;

// ✅ Secure default: render text as text.
export function SafeMessage({ message }: { message: string }) {
  return <p>{message}</p>;
}
```

### Code Example 2
```ts
// Validate security-sensitive state at the boundary.
function isAllowedOrigin(origin: string, allowed: readonly string[]) {
  return allowed.includes(origin);
}

console.log(isAllowedOrigin("https://app.example.com", [
  "https://app.example.com",
]));
```

### Secure Production Example
```ts
type SecurityCheck = {
  name: string;
  passed: boolean;
};

const checks: SecurityCheck[] = [
  { name: "HTTPS", passed: true },
  { name: "Authorization server-side", passed: true },
  { name: "Input validation", passed: true },
  { name: "Security logging", passed: true },
];

console.table(checks);
```

### Vulnerable → Secure
❌ Vulnerable: trust browser-controlled roles, concatenate untrusted HTML/URLs, expose long-lived secrets, or disable browser security controls to make integration easier.  
↓  
✅ Secure: enforce authorization server-side, encode/sanitize untrusted content, use hardened session controls, validate origins/redirects and keep security policies explicit.

### Attack Diagram
```text
Attacker
   ↓
Untrusted Data
   ↓
Weak Boundary
   ↓
Browser / API
   ↓
Unauthorized Action or Data Exposure
```

### Defense Diagram
```text
Input Validation
      ↓
Safe Encoding / Sanitization
      ↓
Browser Policy
      ↓
Server Authorization
      ↓
Monitoring
      ↓
Incident Response
```

### Browser Flow Diagram
```text
Request
  ↓
Origin / Credentials
  ↓
Browser Security Policy
  ↓
Network
  ↓
Server Validation
  ↓
Response
  ↓
Safe DOM / State Handling
```

### Advantages
- Reduced attack surface
- Better separation of trust boundaries
- Easier security testing
- Stronger enterprise governance

### Limitations
- Browser controls vary by capability and deployment
- Security policies can add operational complexity
- Legacy integrations may require migration

### Security Trade-offs
| Control | Benefit | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| HttpOnly cookie | Reduces JS cookie access | Requires CSRF/session design |
| CSP | Limits script execution | Requires policy maintenance |
| Strict CORS | Limits cross-origin access | Integration complexity |
| Strong authorization | Limits privilege | More policy management |
| Dependency pinning | Predictability | Update overhead |

### Best Practices
1. Threat-model the feature before implementation.
2. Enforce authorization on the server.
3. Use HTTPS and secure cookie attributes.
4. Avoid dangerous DOM sinks.
5. Apply CSP and Trusted Types where appropriate.
6. Validate redirects, origins and external URLs.
7. Keep dependencies locked and scanned.
8. Log security-relevant events without leaking secrets.
9. Add security gates to CI/CD.

### Anti-patterns
- Client-only authorization
- `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` for untrusted data
- `eval()` or dynamic code execution
- Storing sensitive long-lived credentials in accessible browser storage without a threat-model justification
- Wildcard credentialed CORS
- Disabling CSP because a third-party script is inconvenient

### Common Mistakes
- Confusing CORS with authentication
- Confusing encoding with authorization
- Logging tokens or passwords
- Assuming HTTPS prevents XSS
- Treating JWT signing as permission enforcement

### Debugging Strategy
1. Reproduce the security behavior in an isolated environment.
2. Inspect Network requests and response headers.
3. Inspect cookies, storage and origin information.
4. Check CSP/console violations.
5. Verify server authorization decisions.
6. Review dependency and build output.
7. Add a regression test for the root cause.

### DevTools Demonstration
- **Network:** inspect request credentials, CORS headers, redirects and security headers.
- **Application:** inspect cookies, storage, service workers and permissions.
- **Console:** inspect CSP, mixed-content and browser-policy violations.
- **Sources:** verify dangerous sinks and generated code.

### Security Checklist
- [ ] Threat model completed
- [ ] Trust boundary identified
- [ ] Server-side authorization enforced
- [ ] Sensitive data minimized
- [ ] Browser security policy configured
- [ ] Dependencies scanned
- [ ] Security tests automated
- [ ] Security logging/alerting configured

### Scenario-Based Interview Question
A production application has a security issue involving **XSS revision**. How would you reproduce it safely, identify the root cause, contain the issue and prevent recurrence?

### Senior Follow-up Questions
1. What is the attacker capability?
2. What is the trust boundary?
3. What browser control can reduce the attack surface?
4. What must be enforced server-side?
5. How would you test the defense?
6. What telemetry would detect recurrence?
7. What is the migration strategy for legacy clients?

At Staff/Principal level, design security as a platform capability: centralized identity, policy enforcement, secure API clients, security headers, dependency governance, audit logging, threat modeling, CI/CD gates and incident response.

- [ ] Authorization is server-side
- [ ] Inputs are untrusted by default
- [ ] Dangerous browser APIs are controlled
- [ ] Third-party code is governed
- [ ] Secrets are not exposed
- [ ] Security policies are versioned

## Question 332 — CSP revision

**Module:** Module 20 – Final Revision  
**Difficulty:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ Principal  
**Experience Level:** 12+ Years  
**Frequently Asked In:** Google • Meta • Amazon • Microsoft • Netflix • Adobe • Atlassian • Stripe • Uber • Airbnb

### Question
How would you explain **CSP revision**, model its threats, implement the defense, and review it for production?

### Definition
**CSP revision** is a frontend security concern that must be evaluated across the browser, application, identity layer, API boundary, dependencies and production operations.

### Overview
Security is a system property. The frontend participates in the attack surface, but sensitive authorization decisions and trust-boundary enforcement must remain server-side.

### Why It Matters
- Prevents account compromise, data exposure and unauthorized actions.
- Reduces exploitable browser and supply-chain attack surface.
- Makes security controls reviewable, testable and observable.

### Browser Behavior
Modern browsers enforce origin boundaries, cookie policies, CSP, permission controls, framing restrictions and secure-context requirements. Security behavior depends on request origin, credentials, headers and browser policy.

### Threat Model
Identify attacker capabilities, protected assets, trust boundaries, entry points, dangerous sinks, authorization decisions and the impact of compromise.

### Attack Flow
```text
Attacker / Untrusted Input
          ↓
      Trust Boundary
          ↓
  Vulnerable Sink / Policy Gap
          ↓
      Security Impact
```

### Internal Security Mechanism
Use browser-enforced controls where possible: Same-Origin Policy, CSP, cookie attributes, CORS, Fetch Metadata, framing protections, Trusted Types and secure transport.

### Architecture
```text
Identity Provider
       ↓
  Secure Session
       ↓
Frontend ─────→ API Gateway
   │                ↓
   └─ Browser       Authorization
      Controls          ↓
                    Backend
```

### Execution Flow
Identify trust boundary → identify attacker-controlled input/state → determine exploit path → apply layered controls → validate with tests and telemetry.

### Real-world Threat
A production application can be exposed when **CSP revision** is implemented as a convenience feature without explicit trust-boundary analysis, secure defaults and regression tests.

### Real-world Defense
Combine browser controls, server-side validation, least privilege, secure identity/session management, dependency governance and monitoring. Never rely on a single client-side check.

### Production Use Cases
Enterprise SPAs, SaaS applications, banking portals, healthcare systems, e-commerce applications, admin consoles and multi-tenant platforms all require layered security around identity, data and browser execution.

### Enterprise Examples
Security architecture should make authentication, authorization, API boundaries, CSP, dependency controls, logging and incident response explicit rather than scattering security assumptions through components.

### Code Example 1
```ts
// Feature-detect Trusted Types before using the API.
const policy = globalThis.trustedTypes?.createPolicy("app", {
  createHTML: (input) => {
    // Production policy should sanitize with an approved sanitizer.
    return input;
  },
});

console.log(Boolean(policy));
```

### Code Example 2
```ts
// Validate security-sensitive state at the boundary.
function isAllowedOrigin(origin: string, allowed: readonly string[]) {
  return allowed.includes(origin);
}

console.log(isAllowedOrigin("https://app.example.com", [
  "https://app.example.com",
]));
```

### Secure Production Example
```ts
type SecurityCheck = {
  name: string;
  passed: boolean;
};

const checks: SecurityCheck[] = [
  { name: "HTTPS", passed: true },
  { name: "Authorization server-side", passed: true },
  { name: "Input validation", passed: true },
  { name: "Security logging", passed: true },
];

console.table(checks);
```

### Vulnerable → Secure
❌ Vulnerable: trust browser-controlled roles, concatenate untrusted HTML/URLs, expose long-lived secrets, or disable browser security controls to make integration easier.  
↓  
✅ Secure: enforce authorization server-side, encode/sanitize untrusted content, use hardened session controls, validate origins/redirects and keep security policies explicit.

### Attack Diagram
```text
Attacker
   ↓
Untrusted Data
   ↓
Weak Boundary
   ↓
Browser / API
   ↓
Unauthorized Action or Data Exposure
```

### Defense Diagram
```text
Input Validation
      ↓
Safe Encoding / Sanitization
      ↓
Browser Policy
      ↓
Server Authorization
      ↓
Monitoring
      ↓
Incident Response
```

### Browser Flow Diagram
```text
Request
  ↓
Origin / Credentials
  ↓
Browser Security Policy
  ↓
Network
  ↓
Server Validation
  ↓
Response
  ↓
Safe DOM / State Handling
```

### Advantages
- Reduced attack surface
- Better separation of trust boundaries
- Easier security testing
- Stronger enterprise governance

### Limitations
- Browser controls vary by capability and deployment
- Security policies can add operational complexity
- Legacy integrations may require migration

### Security Trade-offs
| Control | Benefit | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| HttpOnly cookie | Reduces JS cookie access | Requires CSRF/session design |
| CSP | Limits script execution | Requires policy maintenance |
| Strict CORS | Limits cross-origin access | Integration complexity |
| Strong authorization | Limits privilege | More policy management |
| Dependency pinning | Predictability | Update overhead |

### Best Practices
1. Threat-model the feature before implementation.
2. Enforce authorization on the server.
3. Use HTTPS and secure cookie attributes.
4. Avoid dangerous DOM sinks.
5. Apply CSP and Trusted Types where appropriate.
6. Validate redirects, origins and external URLs.
7. Keep dependencies locked and scanned.
8. Log security-relevant events without leaking secrets.
9. Add security gates to CI/CD.

### Anti-patterns
- Client-only authorization
- `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` for untrusted data
- `eval()` or dynamic code execution
- Storing sensitive long-lived credentials in accessible browser storage without a threat-model justification
- Wildcard credentialed CORS
- Disabling CSP because a third-party script is inconvenient

### Common Mistakes
- Confusing CORS with authentication
- Confusing encoding with authorization
- Logging tokens or passwords
- Assuming HTTPS prevents XSS
- Treating JWT signing as permission enforcement

### Debugging Strategy
1. Reproduce the security behavior in an isolated environment.
2. Inspect Network requests and response headers.
3. Inspect cookies, storage and origin information.
4. Check CSP/console violations.
5. Verify server authorization decisions.
6. Review dependency and build output.
7. Add a regression test for the root cause.

### DevTools Demonstration
- **Network:** inspect request credentials, CORS headers, redirects and security headers.
- **Application:** inspect cookies, storage, service workers and permissions.
- **Console:** inspect CSP, mixed-content and browser-policy violations.
- **Sources:** verify dangerous sinks and generated code.

### Security Checklist
- [ ] Threat model completed
- [ ] Trust boundary identified
- [ ] Server-side authorization enforced
- [ ] Sensitive data minimized
- [ ] Browser security policy configured
- [ ] Dependencies scanned
- [ ] Security tests automated
- [ ] Security logging/alerting configured

7. What is the migration strategy for legacy clients?

- Confusing CORS with authentication
- Confusing encoding with authorization
- Logging tokens or passwords
- Assuming HTTPS prevents XSS
- Treating JWT signing as permission enforcement

### Debugging Strategy
1. Reproduce the security behavior in an isolated environment.
2. Inspect Network requests and response headers.
3. Inspect cookies, storage and origin information.
4. Check CSP/console violations.
5. Verify server authorization decisions.
6. Review dependency and build output.
7. Add a regression test for the root cause.

### DevTools Demonstration
- **Network:** inspect request credentials, CORS headers, redirects and security headers.
- **Application:** inspect cookies, storage, service workers and permissions.
- **Console:** inspect CSP, mixed-content and browser-policy violations.
- **Sources:** verify dangerous sinks and generated code.

- [ ] Trust boundary identified
- [ ] Server-side authorization enforced
- [ ] Sensitive data minimized
- [ ] Browser security policy configured
- [ ] Dependencies scanned

## Question 335 — Security headers revision

**Module:** Module 20 – Final Revision  
**Difficulty:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ Principal  
**Experience Level:** 12+ Years  
**Frequently Asked In:** Google • Meta • Amazon • Microsoft • Netflix • Adobe • Atlassian • Stripe • Uber • Airbnb

### Question
How would you explain **Security headers revision**, model its threats, implement the defense, and review it for production?

### Definition
**Security headers revision** is a frontend security concern that must be evaluated across the browser, application, identity layer, API boundary, dependencies and production operations.

### Overview
Security is a system property. The frontend participates in the attack surface, but sensitive authorization decisions and trust-boundary enforcement must remain server-side.

### Why It Matters
- Prevents account compromise, data exposure and unauthorized actions.
- Reduces exploitable browser and supply-chain attack surface.
- Makes security controls reviewable, testable and observable.

### Browser Behavior
Modern browsers enforce origin boundaries, cookie policies, CSP, permission controls, framing restrictions and secure-context requirements. Security behavior depends on request origin, credentials, headers and browser policy.

### Threat Model
Identify attacker capabilities, protected assets, trust boundaries, entry points, dangerous sinks, authorization decisions and the impact of compromise.

### Attack Flow
```text
Attacker / Untrusted Input
          ↓
      Trust Boundary
          ↓
  Vulnerable Sink / Policy Gap
          ↓
      Security Impact
```

### Internal Security Mechanism
Use browser-enforced controls where possible: Same-Origin Policy, CSP, cookie attributes, CORS, Fetch Metadata, framing protections, Trusted Types and secure transport.

### Architecture
```text
Identity Provider
       ↓
  Secure Session
       ↓
Frontend ─────→ API Gateway
   │                ↓
   └─ Browser       Authorization
      Controls          ↓
                    Backend
```

### Execution Flow
Identify trust boundary → identify attacker-controlled input/state → determine exploit path → apply layered controls → validate with tests and telemetry.

### Real-world Threat
A production application can be exposed when **Security headers revision** is implemented as a convenience feature without explicit trust-boundary analysis, secure defaults and regression tests.

### Real-world Defense
Combine browser controls, server-side validation, least privilege, secure identity/session management, dependency governance and monitoring. Never rely on a single client-side check.

### Production Use Cases
Enterprise SPAs, SaaS applications, banking portals, healthcare systems, e-commerce applications, admin consoles and multi-tenant platforms all require layered security around identity, data and browser execution.

### Enterprise Examples
Security architecture should make authentication, authorization, API boundaries, CSP, dependency controls, logging and incident response explicit rather than scattering security assumptions through components.

### Code Example 1
```ts
// Secure-by-default API wrapper: never interpolate secrets into URLs.
export async function getJson<T>(url: string): Promise<T> {
  const response = await fetch(url, {
    credentials: "same-origin",
    headers: { Accept: "application/json" },
  });

  if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${response.status}`);
  return response.json() as Promise<T>;
}
```

### Code Example 2
```ts
// Validate security-sensitive state at the boundary.
function isAllowedOrigin(origin: string, allowed: readonly string[]) {
  return allowed.includes(origin);
}

console.log(isAllowedOrigin("https://app.example.com", [
  "https://app.example.com",
]));
```

### Secure Production Example
```ts
type SecurityCheck = {
  name: string;
  passed: boolean;
};

const checks: SecurityCheck[] = [
  { name: "HTTPS", passed: true },
  { name: "Authorization server-side", passed: true },
  { name: "Input validation", passed: true },
  { name: "Security logging", passed: true },
];

console.table(checks);
```

### Vulnerable → Secure
❌ Vulnerable: trust browser-controlled roles, concatenate untrusted HTML/URLs, expose long-lived secrets, or disable browser security controls to make integration easier.  
↓  
✅ Secure: enforce authorization server-side, encode/sanitize untrusted content, use hardened session controls, validate origins/redirects and keep security policies explicit.

### Attack Diagram
```text
Attacker
   ↓
Untrusted Data
   ↓
Weak Boundary
   ↓
Browser / API
   ↓
Unauthorized Action or Data Exposure
```

### Defense Diagram
```text
Input Validation
      ↓
Safe Encoding / Sanitization
      ↓
Browser Policy
      ↓
Server Authorization
      ↓
Monitoring
      ↓
Incident Response
```

### Browser Flow Diagram
```text
Request
  ↓
Origin / Credentials
  ↓
Browser Security Policy
  ↓
Network
  ↓
Server Validation
  ↓
Response
  ↓
Safe DOM / State Handling
```

### Advantages
- Reduced attack surface
- Better separation of trust boundaries
- Easier security testing
- Stronger enterprise governance

### Limitations
- Browser controls vary by capability and deployment
- Security policies can add operational complexity
- Legacy integrations may require migration

### Security Trade-offs
| Control | Benefit | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| HttpOnly cookie | Reduces JS cookie access | Requires CSRF/session design |
| CSP | Limits script execution | Requires policy maintenance |
| Strict CORS | Limits cross-origin access | Integration complexity |
| Strong authorization | Limits privilege | More policy management |
| Dependency pinning | Predictability | Update overhead |

### Best Practices
1. Threat-model the feature before implementation.
2. Enforce authorization on the server.
3. Use HTTPS and secure cookie attributes.
4. Avoid dangerous DOM sinks.
5. Apply CSP and Trusted Types where appropriate.
6. Validate redirects, origins and external URLs.
7. Keep dependencies locked and scanned.
8. Log security-relevant events without leaking secrets.
9. Add security gates to CI/CD.

### Anti-patterns
- Client-only authorization
- `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` for untrusted data
- `eval()` or dynamic code execution
- Storing sensitive long-lived credentials in accessible browser storage without a threat-model justification
- Wildcard credentialed CORS
- Disabling CSP because a third-party script is inconvenient

### Common Mistakes
- Confusing CORS with authentication
- Confusing encoding with authorization
- Logging tokens or passwords
- Assuming HTTPS prevents XSS
- Treating JWT signing as permission enforcement

### Debugging Strategy
1. Reproduce the security behavior in an isolated environment.
2. Inspect Network requests and response headers.
3. Inspect cookies, storage and origin information.
4. Check CSP/console violations.
5. Verify server authorization decisions.
6. Review dependency and build output.
7. Add a regression test for the root cause.

### DevTools Demonstration
- **Network:** inspect request credentials, CORS headers, redirects and security headers.
- **Application:** inspect cookies, storage, service workers and permissions.
- **Console:** inspect CSP, mixed-content and browser-policy violations.
- **Sources:** verify dangerous sinks and generated code.

### Security Checklist
- [ ] Threat model completed
- [ ] Trust boundary identified
- [ ] Server-side authorization enforced
- [ ] Sensitive data minimized
- [ ] Browser security policy configured
- [ ] Dependencies scanned
- [ ] Security tests automated
- [ ] Security logging/alerting configured

4. What must be enforced server-side?
5. How would you test the defense?
6. What telemetry would detect recurrence?
7. What is the migration strategy for legacy clients?

```ts

  return allowed.includes(origin);
}

console.log(isAllowedOrigin("https://app.example.com", [
  "https://app.example.com",
```

### Secure Production Example
```ts
type SecurityCheck = {
  name: string;
  passed: boolean;
};

const checks: SecurityCheck[] = [
  { name: "HTTPS", passed: true },
  { name: "Authorization server-side", passed: true },
  { name: "Input validation", passed: true },
  { name: "Security logging", passed: true },
];

console.table(checks);
```

### Vulnerable → Secure
❌ Vulnerable: trust browser-controlled roles, concatenate untrusted HTML/URLs, expose long-lived secrets, or disable browser security controls to make integration easier.  
↓  
✅ Secure: enforce authorization server-side, encode/sanitize untrusted content, use hardened session controls, validate origins/redirects and keep security policies explicit.

### Attack Diagram
```text
Attacker
   ↓
Untrusted Data
   ↓
Weak Boundary
   ↓
Browser / API
   ↓
Unauthorized Action or Data Exposure
```

### Defense Diagram
```text
Input Validation
      ↓
Safe Encoding / Sanitization
      ↓
Browser Policy
      ↓
Server Authorization
      ↓
Monitoring
      ↓
Incident Response
```

### Browser Flow Diagram
```text
Request
  ↓
Origin / Credentials
  ↓
Browser Security Policy
  ↓
Network
  ↓
Server Validation
  ↓
Response
  ↓
Safe DOM / State Handling
```

### Advantages
- Reduced attack surface
- Better separation of trust boundaries
- Easier security testing
- Stronger enterprise governance

### Limitations
- Browser controls vary by capability and deployment
- Security policies can add operational complexity
- Legacy integrations may require migration

### Security Trade-offs
| Control | Benefit | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| HttpOnly cookie | Reduces JS cookie access | Requires CSRF/session design |
| CSP | Limits script execution | Requires policy maintenance |
| Strict CORS | Limits cross-origin access | Integration complexity |
| Strong authorization | Limits privilege | More policy management |
| Dependency pinning | Predictability | Update overhead |

### Best Practices
1. Threat-model the feature before implementation.
2. Enforce authorization on the server.
3. Use HTTPS and secure cookie attributes.
4. Avoid dangerous DOM sinks.
5. Apply CSP and Trusted Types where appropriate.
6. Validate redirects, origins and external URLs.
7. Keep dependencies locked and scanned.
8. Log security-relevant events without leaking secrets.
9. Add security gates to CI/CD.

### Anti-patterns
- Client-only authorization
- `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` for untrusted data
- `eval()` or dynamic code execution
- Storing sensitive long-lived credentials in accessible browser storage without a threat-model justification
- Wildcard credentialed CORS
- Disabling CSP because a third-party script is inconvenient

### Common Mistakes
- Confusing CORS with authentication
- Confusing encoding with authorization
- Logging tokens or passwords
- Assuming HTTPS prevents XSS
- Treating JWT signing as permission enforcement

### Debugging Strategy
1. Reproduce the security behavior in an isolated environment.
2. Inspect Network requests and response headers.
3. Inspect cookies, storage and origin information.
4. Check CSP/console violations.
5. Verify server authorization decisions.
6. Review dependency and build output.
7. Add a regression test for the root cause.

### DevTools Demonstration
- **Network:** inspect request credentials, CORS headers, redirects and security headers.
- **Application:** inspect cookies, storage, service workers and permissions.
- **Console:** inspect CSP, mixed-content and browser-policy violations.
- **Sources:** verify dangerous sinks and generated code.

### Security Checklist
- [ ] Threat model completed
- [ ] Trust boundary identified
- [ ] Server-side authorization enforced
- [ ] Sensitive data minimized
- [ ] Browser security policy configured
- [ ] Dependencies scanned
- [ ] Security tests automated
- [ ] Security logging/alerting configured

## Question 338 — Supply-chain revision

**Module:** Module 20 – Final Revision  
**Difficulty:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ Principal

**Frequently Asked In:** Google • Meta • Amazon • Microsoft • Netflix • Adobe • Atlassian • Stripe • Uber • Airbnb

### Question
How would you explain **Supply-chain revision**, model its threats, implement the defense, and review it for production?

### Definition
**Supply-chain revision** is a frontend security concern that must be evaluated across the browser, application, identity layer, API boundary, dependencies and production operations.

### Overview
Security is a system property. The frontend participates in the attack surface, but sensitive authorization decisions and trust-boundary enforcement must remain server-side.

### Why It Matters
- Prevents account compromise, data exposure and unauthorized actions.
- Reduces exploitable browser and supply-chain attack surface.
- Makes security controls reviewable, testable and observable.

### Browser Behavior
Modern browsers enforce origin boundaries, cookie policies, CSP, permission controls, framing restrictions and secure-context requirements. Security behavior depends on request origin, credentials, headers and browser policy.

### Threat Model
Identify attacker capabilities, protected assets, trust boundaries, entry points, dangerous sinks, authorization decisions and the impact of compromise.

### Attack Flow
```text
Attacker / Untrusted Input
          ↓
      Trust Boundary
          ↓
  Vulnerable Sink / Policy Gap
          ↓
      Security Impact
```

### Internal Security Mechanism
Use browser-enforced controls where possible: Same-Origin Policy, CSP, cookie attributes, CORS, Fetch Metadata, framing protections, Trusted Types and secure transport.

### Architecture
```text
Identity Provider
       ↓

       ↓
Frontend ─────→ API Gateway
   │                ↓
   └─ Browser       Authorization
      Controls          ↓
                    Backend
```

### Execution Flow
Identify trust boundary → identify attacker-controlled input/state → determine exploit path → apply layered controls → validate with tests and telemetry.

### Real-world Threat
A production application can be exposed when **Supply-chain revision** is implemented as a convenience feature without explicit trust-boundary analysis, secure defaults and regression tests.

### Real-world Defense
Combine browser controls, server-side validation, least privilege, secure identity/session management, dependency governance and monitoring. Never rely on a single client-side check.

### Production Use Cases
Enterprise SPAs, SaaS applications, banking portals, healthcare systems, e-commerce applications, admin consoles and multi-tenant platforms all require layered security around identity, data and browser execution.

```ts
}
```

## Question 340 — React security revision

**Module:** Module 20 – Final Revision  
**Difficulty:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ Principal  
**Experience Level:** 12+ Years  
**Frequently Asked In:** Google • Meta • Amazon • Microsoft • Netflix • Adobe • Atlassian • Stripe • Uber • Airbnb

### Question
How would you explain **React security revision**, model its threats, implement the defense, and review it for production?

### Definition
**React security revision** is a frontend security concern that must be evaluated across the browser, application, identity layer, API boundary, dependencies and production operations.

### Overview
Security is a system property. The frontend participates in the attack surface, but sensitive authorization decisions and trust-boundary enforcement must remain server-side.

### Why It Matters
- Prevents account compromise, data exposure and unauthorized actions.
- Reduces exploitable browser and supply-chain attack surface.
- Makes security controls reviewable, testable and observable.

### Browser Behavior
Modern browsers enforce origin boundaries, cookie policies, CSP, permission controls, framing restrictions and secure-context requirements. Security behavior depends on request origin, credentials, headers and browser policy.

### Threat Model
Identify attacker capabilities, protected assets, trust boundaries, entry points, dangerous sinks, authorization decisions and the impact of compromise.

### Attack Flow
```text
Attacker / Untrusted Input
          ↓
      Trust Boundary
          ↓
  Vulnerable Sink / Policy Gap
          ↓
      Security Impact
```

### Internal Security Mechanism
Use browser-enforced controls where possible: Same-Origin Policy, CSP, cookie attributes, CORS, Fetch Metadata, framing protections, Trusted Types and secure transport.

### Architecture
```text
Identity Provider
       ↓
  Secure Session
       ↓
Frontend ─────→ API Gateway
   │                ↓
   └─ Browser       Authorization
      Controls          ↓
                    Backend
```

### Execution Flow
Identify trust boundary → identify attacker-controlled input/state → determine exploit path → apply layered controls → validate with tests and telemetry.

### Real-world Threat
A production application can be exposed when **React security revision** is implemented as a convenience feature without explicit trust-boundary analysis, secure defaults and regression tests.

### Real-world Defense
Combine browser controls, server-side validation, least privilege, secure identity/session management, dependency governance and monitoring. Never rely on a single client-side check.

### Production Use Cases
Enterprise SPAs, SaaS applications, banking portals, healthcare systems, e-commerce applications, admin consoles and multi-tenant platforms all require layered security around identity, data and browser execution.

### Enterprise Examples
Security architecture should make authentication, authorization, API boundaries, CSP, dependency controls, logging and incident response explicit rather than scattering security assumptions through components.

### Code Example 1
```ts
// Secure-by-default API wrapper: never interpolate secrets into URLs.
export async function getJson<T>(url: string): Promise<T> {
  const response = await fetch(url, {
    credentials: "same-origin",
    headers: { Accept: "application/json" },
  });

  if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${response.status}`);
  return response.json() as Promise<T>;
}
```

### Code Example 2
```ts
// Validate security-sensitive state at the boundary.
function isAllowedOrigin(origin: string, allowed: readonly string[]) {
  return allowed.includes(origin);
}

console.log(isAllowedOrigin("https://app.example.com", [
  "https://app.example.com",
]));
```

### Secure Production Example
```ts
type SecurityCheck = {
  name: string;
  passed: boolean;
};

const checks: SecurityCheck[] = [
  { name: "HTTPS", passed: true },
  { name: "Authorization server-side", passed: true },
  { name: "Input validation", passed: true },
  { name: "Security logging", passed: true },
];

console.table(checks);
```

### Vulnerable → Secure
❌ Vulnerable: trust browser-controlled roles, concatenate untrusted HTML/URLs, expose long-lived secrets, or disable browser security controls to make integration easier.  
↓  
✅ Secure: enforce authorization server-side, encode/sanitize untrusted content, use hardened session controls, validate origins/redirects and keep security policies explicit.

### Attack Diagram
```text
Attacker
   ↓
Untrusted Data
   ↓
Weak Boundary
   ↓
Browser / API
   ↓
Unauthorized Action or Data Exposure
```

### Defense Diagram
```text
Input Validation
      ↓
Safe Encoding / Sanitization
      ↓
Browser Policy
      ↓
Server Authorization
      ↓
Monitoring
      ↓
Incident Response
```

### Browser Flow Diagram
```text
Request
  ↓
Origin / Credentials
  ↓
Browser Security Policy
  ↓
Network
  ↓
Server Validation
  ↓
Response
  ↓
Safe DOM / State Handling
```

### Advantages
- Reduced attack surface
- Better separation of trust boundaries
- Easier security testing
- Stronger enterprise governance

### Limitations
- Browser controls vary by capability and deployment
- Security policies can add operational complexity
- Legacy integrations may require migration

### Security Trade-offs
| Control | Benefit | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| HttpOnly cookie | Reduces JS cookie access | Requires CSRF/session design |
| CSP | Limits script execution | Requires policy maintenance |
| Strict CORS | Limits cross-origin access | Integration complexity |
| Strong authorization | Limits privilege | More policy management |
| Dependency pinning | Predictability | Update overhead |

### Best Practices
1. Threat-model the feature before implementation.
2. Enforce authorization on the server.
3. Use HTTPS and secure cookie attributes.
4. Avoid dangerous DOM sinks.
5. Apply CSP and Trusted Types where appropriate.
6. Validate redirects, origins and external URLs.
7. Keep dependencies locked and scanned.
8. Log security-relevant events without leaking secrets.
9. Add security gates to CI/CD.

### Anti-patterns
- Client-only authorization
- `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` for untrusted data
- `eval()` or dynamic code execution
- Storing sensitive long-lived credentials in accessible browser storage without a threat-model justification
- Wildcard credentialed CORS
- Disabling CSP because a third-party script is inconvenient

### Common Mistakes
- Confusing CORS with authentication
- Confusing encoding with authorization
- Logging tokens or passwords
- Assuming HTTPS prevents XSS
- Treating JWT signing as permission enforcement

### Debugging Strategy
1. Reproduce the security behavior in an isolated environment.
2. Inspect Network requests and response headers.
3. Inspect cookies, storage and origin information.
4. Check CSP/console violations.
5. Verify server authorization decisions.
6. Review dependency and build output.
7. Add a regression test for the root cause.

### DevTools Demonstration
- **Network:** inspect request credentials, CORS headers, redirects and security headers.
- **Application:** inspect cookies, storage, service workers and permissions.
- **Console:** inspect CSP, mixed-content and browser-policy violations.
- **Sources:** verify dangerous sinks and generated code.

### Security Checklist
- [ ] Threat model completed
- [ ] Trust boundary identified
- [ ] Server-side authorization enforced
- [ ] Sensitive data minimized
- [ ] Browser security policy configured
- [ ] Dependencies scanned
- [ ] Security tests automated
- [ ] Security logging/alerting configured

### Scenario-Based Interview Question
A production application has a security issue involving **React security revision**. How would you reproduce it safely, identify the root cause, contain the issue and prevent recurrence?

### Senior Follow-up Questions
1. What is the attacker capability?
2. What is the trust boundary?
3. What browser control can reduce the attack surface?
4. What must be enforced server-side?
5. How would you test the defense?
6. What telemetry would detect recurrence?
7. What is the migration strategy for legacy clients?

### Enterprise Architecture Discussion
At Staff/Principal level, design security as a platform capability: centralized identity, policy enforcement, secure API clients, security headers, dependency governance, audit logging, threat modeling, CI/CD gates and incident response.

### Security Review Checklist
- [ ] Authentication is explicit
- [ ] Authorization is server-side
- [ ] Inputs are untrusted by default
- [ ] Dangerous browser APIs are controlled
- [ ] Third-party code is governed
- [ ] Secrets are not exposed
- [ ] Security policies are versioned

### 30-second Interview Answer
For **React security revision**, I would first identify the attacker and trust boundary, then apply browser and server-side controls in layers. I would validate the defense with automated security tests and monitor production for regression.

### 2-minute Interview Answer
I treat **React security revision** as a threat-modeling problem rather than a code-only problem. I identify attacker capabilities, data flows and trust boundaries, choose secure browser/platform controls, enforce sensitive decisions server-side, test abuse cases, and add CI/CD and production monitoring.

### 5-minute Deep Explanation
At Staff/Principal level, discuss **React security revision** through identity, browser isolation, API boundaries, secure coding, supply-chain risk, observability, incident response, compliance and organizational governance. The strongest answer explains not just the mitigation but its limitations, operational trade-offs and how the organization prevents recurrence.

### Assignments
Create a threat model for a feature involving **React security revision**, list attacker capabilities, trust boundaries, attack paths, mitigations and residual risk.

### Mini Project
Build a secure React 19 + TypeScript application with authenticated routes, server-enforced authorization, hardened session handling, CSP, safe rendering, secure API calls, dependency scanning and security event logging.

### MCQs
1. Where should authorization ultimately be enforced?  
A. CSS  B. Client router only  C. Server/API  D. Browser local state  
**Answer: C**
2. Which cookie attribute prevents JavaScript access?  
A. Secure  B. HttpOnly  C. Path  D. Domain  
**Answer: B**
3. Which control reduces script injection impact?  
A. CSP  B. DNS  C. JSON.parse only  D. CORS alone  
**Answer: A**
4. What is a major supply-chain defense?  
A. Ignore lock files  B. Dependency scanning and provenance  C. Disable HTTPS  D. Remove tests  
**Answer: B**
5. What is the safest assumption for external input?  
A. Trusted  B. Encoded already  C. Untrusted  D. Internal  
**Answer: C**

### Hands-on Exercise
Audit a demo application for **React security revision**. Document the vulnerable trust boundary, reproduce the issue safely, apply a defense and add a regression test.

### Secure Coding Exercise
Implement one secure boundary: validate an origin/redirect, render untrusted text safely, enforce a permission check server-side, or configure a hardened session policy.

### Revision Notes
- React security revision: attacker → trust boundary → exploit → impact → layered defense → test → monitor.
- Browser security controls complement—not replace—server-side authorization.
- Security must survive deployment, dependency updates and production incidents.

### Cheat Sheet
**Identity → Authorization → Transport → Browser Policy → Safe Input/Output → API Validation → Dependencies → Monitoring.**

## Question 343 — Enterprise architecture revision

**Module:** Module 20 – Final Revision  
**Difficulty:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ Principal  
**Experience Level:** 12+ Years  
**Frequently Asked In:** Google • Meta • Amazon • Microsoft • Netflix • Adobe • Atlassian • Stripe • Uber • Airbnb

### Question
How would you explain **Enterprise architecture revision**, model its threats, implement the defense, and review it for production?

### Definition
**Enterprise architecture revision** is a frontend security concern that must be evaluated across the browser, application, identity layer, API boundary, dependencies and production operations.

### Overview
Security is a system property. The frontend participates in the attack surface, but sensitive authorization decisions and trust-boundary enforcement must remain server-side.

### Why It Matters
- Prevents account compromise, data exposure and unauthorized actions.
- Reduces exploitable browser and supply-chain attack surface.
- Makes security controls reviewable, testable and observable.

### Browser Behavior
Modern browsers enforce origin boundaries, cookie policies, CSP, permission controls, framing restrictions and secure-context requirements. Security behavior depends on request origin, credentials, headers and browser policy.

### Threat Model
Identify attacker capabilities, protected assets, trust boundaries, entry points, dangerous sinks, authorization decisions and the impact of compromise.

### Attack Flow
```text
Attacker / Untrusted Input
          ↓
      Trust Boundary
          ↓
  Vulnerable Sink / Policy Gap
          ↓
      Security Impact
```

### Internal Security Mechanism
Use browser-enforced controls where possible: Same-Origin Policy, CSP, cookie attributes, CORS, Fetch Metadata, framing protections, Trusted Types and secure transport.

### Architecture
```text
Identity Provider
       ↓
  Secure Session
       ↓
Frontend ─────→ API Gateway
   │                ↓
   └─ Browser       Authorization
      Controls          ↓
                    Backend
```

### Execution Flow
Identify trust boundary → identify attacker-controlled input/state → determine exploit path → apply layered controls → validate with tests and telemetry.

### Real-world Threat
A production application can be exposed when **Enterprise architecture revision** is implemented as a convenience feature without explicit trust-boundary analysis, secure defaults and regression tests.

### Real-world Defense
Combine browser controls, server-side validation, least privilege, secure identity/session management, dependency governance and monitoring. Never rely on a single client-side check.

### Production Use Cases
Enterprise SPAs, SaaS applications, banking portals, healthcare systems, e-commerce applications, admin consoles and multi-tenant platforms all require layered security around identity, data and browser execution.

### Enterprise Examples
Security architecture should make authentication, authorization, API boundaries, CSP, dependency controls, logging and incident response explicit rather than scattering security assumptions through components.

### Code Example 1
```ts
// Secure-by-default API wrapper: never interpolate secrets into URLs.
export async function getJson<T>(url: string): Promise<T> {
  const response = await fetch(url, {
    credentials: "same-origin",
    headers: { Accept: "application/json" },
  });

  if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${response.status}`);
  return response.json() as Promise<T>;
}
```

### Code Example 2
```ts
// Validate security-sensitive state at the boundary.
function isAllowedOrigin(origin: string, allowed: readonly string[]) {
  return allowed.includes(origin);
}

console.log(isAllowedOrigin("https://app.example.com", [
  "https://app.example.com",
]));
```

### Secure Production Example
```ts
type SecurityCheck = {
  name: string;
  passed: boolean;
};

const checks: SecurityCheck[] = [
  { name: "HTTPS", passed: true },
  { name: "Authorization server-side", passed: true },
  { name: "Input validation", passed: true },
  { name: "Security logging", passed: true },
];

console.table(checks);
```

### Vulnerable → Secure
❌ Vulnerable: trust browser-controlled roles, concatenate untrusted HTML/URLs, expose long-lived secrets, or disable browser security controls to make integration easier.  
↓  
✅ Secure: enforce authorization server-side, encode/sanitize untrusted content, use hardened session controls, validate origins/redirects and keep security policies explicit.

### Attack Diagram
```text
Attacker
   ↓
Untrusted Data
   ↓
Weak Boundary
   ↓
Browser / API
   ↓
Unauthorized Action or Data Exposure
```

### Defense Diagram
```text
Input Validation
      ↓
Safe Encoding / Sanitization
      ↓
Browser Policy
      ↓
Server Authorization
      ↓
Monitoring
      ↓
Incident Response
```

### Browser Flow Diagram
```text
Request
  ↓
Origin / Credentials
  ↓
Browser Security Policy
  ↓
Network
  ↓
Server Validation
  ↓
Response
  ↓
Safe DOM / State Handling
```

### Advantages
- Reduced attack surface
- Better separation of trust boundaries
- Easier security testing
- Stronger enterprise governance

### Limitations
- Browser controls vary by capability and deployment
- Security policies can add operational complexity
- Legacy integrations may require migration

### Security Trade-offs
| Control | Benefit | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| HttpOnly cookie | Reduces JS cookie access | Requires CSRF/session design |
| CSP | Limits script execution | Requires policy maintenance |
| Strict CORS | Limits cross-origin access | Integration complexity |
| Strong authorization | Limits privilege | More policy management |
| Dependency pinning | Predictability | Update overhead |

### Best Practices
1. Threat-model the feature before implementation.
2. Enforce authorization on the server.
3. Use HTTPS and secure cookie attributes.
4. Avoid dangerous DOM sinks.
5. Apply CSP and Trusted Types where appropriate.
6. Validate redirects, origins and external URLs.
7. Keep dependencies locked and scanned.
8. Log security-relevant events without leaking secrets.
9. Add security gates to CI/CD.

### Anti-patterns
- Client-only authorization
- `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` for untrusted data
- `eval()` or dynamic code execution
- Storing sensitive long-lived credentials in accessible browser storage without a threat-model justification
- Wildcard credentialed CORS
- Disabling CSP because a third-party script is inconvenient

### Common Mistakes
- Confusing CORS with authentication
- Confusing encoding with authorization
- Logging tokens or passwords
- Assuming HTTPS prevents XSS
- Treating JWT signing as permission enforcement

### Debugging Strategy
1. Reproduce the security behavior in an isolated environment.
2. Inspect Network requests and response headers.
3. Inspect cookies, storage and origin information.
4. Check CSP/console violations.
5. Verify server authorization decisions.
6. Review dependency and build output.
7. Add a regression test for the root cause.

### DevTools Demonstration
- **Network:** inspect request credentials, CORS headers, redirects and security headers.
- **Application:** inspect cookies, storage, service workers and permissions.
- **Console:** inspect CSP, mixed-content and browser-policy violations.
- **Sources:** verify dangerous sinks and generated code.

### Security Checklist
- [ ] Threat model completed
- [ ] Trust boundary identified
- [ ] Server-side authorization enforced
- [ ] Sensitive data minimized
- [ ] Browser security policy configured
- [ ] Dependencies scanned
- [ ] Security tests automated
- [ ] Security logging/alerting configured

### Scenario-Based Interview Question
A production application has a security issue involving **Enterprise architecture revision**. How would you reproduce it safely, identify the root cause, contain the issue and prevent recurrence?

### Senior Follow-up Questions
1. What is the attacker capability?
2. What is the trust boundary?
3. What browser control can reduce the attack surface?
4. What must be enforced server-side?
5. How would you test the defense?
6. What telemetry would detect recurrence?
7. What is the migration strategy for legacy clients?

### Enterprise Architecture Discussion

- [ ] Inputs are untrusted by default

- [ ] Third-party code is governed
- [ ] Secrets are not exposed
- [ ] Security policies are versioned

✅ Secure: enforce authorization server-side, encode/sanitize untrusted content, use hardened session controls, validate origins/redirects and keep security policies explicit.

### Attack Diagram
```text
Attacker
   ↓
Untrusted Data
   ↓
Weak Boundary
   ↓
Browser / API
   ↓
Unauthorized Action or Data Exposure
```

### Defense Diagram
```text
Input Validation
      ↓
Safe Encoding / Sanitization
      ↓
Browser Policy
      ↓
Server Authorization
      ↓
Monitoring
      ↓
Incident Response
```

### Browser Flow Diagram
```text
Request
  ↓
Origin / Credentials
  ↓
Browser Security Policy
  ↓
Network
  ↓
Server Validation
  ↓
Response
  ↓
Safe DOM / State Handling
```

### Advantages
- Reduced attack surface
- Better separation of trust boundaries
- Easier security testing
- Stronger enterprise governance

### Limitations
- Browser controls vary by capability and deployment
- Security policies can add operational complexity
- Legacy integrations may require migration

### Security Trade-offs
| Control | Benefit | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| HttpOnly cookie | Reduces JS cookie access | Requires CSRF/session design |
| CSP | Limits script execution | Requires policy maintenance |
| Strict CORS | Limits cross-origin access | Integration complexity |
| Strong authorization | Limits privilege | More policy management |
| Dependency pinning | Predictability | Update overhead |

### Best Practices
1. Threat-model the feature before implementation.
2. Enforce authorization on the server.
3. Use HTTPS and secure cookie attributes.
4. Avoid dangerous DOM sinks.
5. Apply CSP and Trusted Types where appropriate.
6. Validate redirects, origins and external URLs.
7. Keep dependencies locked and scanned.
8. Log security-relevant events without leaking secrets.
9. Add security gates to CI/CD.

### Anti-patterns
- Client-only authorization
- `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` for untrusted data
- `eval()` or dynamic code execution
- Storing sensitive long-lived credentials in accessible browser storage without a threat-model justification
- Wildcard credentialed CORS
- Disabling CSP because a third-party script is inconvenient

### Common Mistakes
- Confusing CORS with authentication
- Confusing encoding with authorization
- Logging tokens or passwords
- Assuming HTTPS prevents XSS
- Treating JWT signing as permission enforcement

### Debugging Strategy
1. Reproduce the security behavior in an isolated environment.
2. Inspect Network requests and response headers.
3. Inspect cookies, storage and origin information.
4. Check CSP/console violations.
5. Verify server authorization decisions.
6. Review dependency and build output.
7. Add a regression test for the root cause.

### DevTools Demonstration
- **Network:** inspect request credentials, CORS headers, redirects and security headers.
- **Application:** inspect cookies, storage, service workers and permissions.
- **Console:** inspect CSP, mixed-content and browser-policy violations.
- **Sources:** verify dangerous sinks and generated code.

### Security Checklist
- [ ] Threat model completed
- [ ] Trust boundary identified
- [ ] Server-side authorization enforced
- [ ] Sensitive data minimized
- [ ] Browser security policy configured
- [ ] Dependencies scanned
- [ ] Security tests automated
- [ ] Security logging/alerting configured

A production application has a security issue involving **Final security assessment**. How would you reproduce it safely, identify the root cause, contain the issue and prevent recurrence?

### Senior Follow-up Questions

2. What is the trust boundary?
3. What browser control can reduce the attack surface?
4. What must be enforced server-side?
5. How would you test the defense?
6. What telemetry would detect recurrence?
7. What is the migration strategy for legacy clients?

### Enterprise Architecture Discussion

- [ ] Authorization is server-side
- [ ] Inputs are untrusted by default

- [ ] Third-party code is governed
- [ ] Secrets are not exposed
- [ ] Security policies are versioned

## Question 346 — Top OWASP questions

**Module:** Module 20 – Final Revision  
**Difficulty:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ Principal  
**Experience Level:** 12+ Years  
**Frequently Asked In:** Google • Meta • Amazon • Microsoft • Netflix • Adobe • Atlassian • Stripe • Uber • Airbnb

### Question
How would you explain **Top OWASP questions**, model its threats, implement the defense, and review it for production?

### Definition
**Top OWASP questions** is a frontend security concern that must be evaluated across the browser, application, identity layer, API boundary, dependencies and production operations.

### Overview
Security is a system property. The frontend participates in the attack surface, but sensitive authorization decisions and trust-boundary enforcement must remain server-side.

### Why It Matters
- Prevents account compromise, data exposure and unauthorized actions.
- Reduces exploitable browser and supply-chain attack surface.
- Makes security controls reviewable, testable and observable.

### Browser Behavior
Modern browsers enforce origin boundaries, cookie policies, CSP, permission controls, framing restrictions and secure-context requirements. Security behavior depends on request origin, credentials, headers and browser policy.

### Threat Model
Identify attacker capabilities, protected assets, trust boundaries, entry points, dangerous sinks, authorization decisions and the impact of compromise.

### Attack Flow
```text
Attacker / Untrusted Input
          ↓
      Trust Boundary
          ↓
  Vulnerable Sink / Policy Gap
          ↓
      Security Impact
```

### Internal Security Mechanism
Use browser-enforced controls where possible: Same-Origin Policy, CSP, cookie attributes, CORS, Fetch Metadata, framing protections, Trusted Types and secure transport.

### Architecture
```text
Identity Provider
       ↓
  Secure Session
       ↓
Frontend ─────→ API Gateway
   │                ↓
   └─ Browser       Authorization
      Controls          ↓
                    Backend
```

### Execution Flow
Identify trust boundary → identify attacker-controlled input/state → determine exploit path → apply layered controls → validate with tests and telemetry.

### Real-world Threat
A production application can be exposed when **Top OWASP questions** is implemented as a convenience feature without explicit trust-boundary analysis, secure defaults and regression tests.

### Real-world Defense
Combine browser controls, server-side validation, least privilege, secure identity/session management, dependency governance and monitoring. Never rely on a single client-side check.

### Production Use Cases
Enterprise SPAs, SaaS applications, banking portals, healthcare systems, e-commerce applications, admin consoles and multi-tenant platforms all require layered security around identity, data and browser execution.

### Enterprise Examples
Security architecture should make authentication, authorization, API boundaries, CSP, dependency controls, logging and incident response explicit rather than scattering security assumptions through components.

### Code Example 1
```ts
// Secure-by-default API wrapper: never interpolate secrets into URLs.
export async function getJson<T>(url: string): Promise<T> {
  const response = await fetch(url, {
    credentials: "same-origin",
    headers: { Accept: "application/json" },
  });

  if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${response.status}`);
  return response.json() as Promise<T>;
}
```

### Code Example 2
```ts
// Validate security-sensitive state at the boundary.
function isAllowedOrigin(origin: string, allowed: readonly string[]) {
  return allowed.includes(origin);
}

console.log(isAllowedOrigin("https://app.example.com", [
  "https://app.example.com",
]));
```

```ts
  name: string;
  passed: boolean;
};

  { name: "HTTPS", passed: true },
  { name: "Authorization server-side", passed: true },
  { name: "Input validation", passed: true },
  { name: "Security logging", passed: true },
];

console.table(checks);
```

   ↓


```text
      ↓

      ↓

      ↓
Incident Response
```

### Browser Flow Diagram

```text
Request
  ↓
Origin / Credentials
  ↓
Browser Security Policy
  ↓
Network
  ↓

  ↓

  ↓
```
